db0-why.name: What is a database and why not just use files?
db0-why.desc: A database is an organized collection of structured data managed by a DBMS. Files work for tiny projects but break down fast — no fast search, no concurrent access, no integrity rules.
db0-why.q: What is a database? Why do we need one instead of just using files?
db0-why.qsub: What happens when two users try to write to the same CSV file at the same time?
db0-why.what:
Database = structured data collection that a DBMS (such as PostgreSQL) manages. Files (CSV/JSON) are fine for small tasks, but they fail immediately in a real application.

Files have four problems: search slow (the entire file must be read), concurrency unsafe (if two people write at the same time the data gets corrupted), no integrity (no rules — duplicate or broken data can appear easily), and no scale. Database solves all of these: index (fast search), locking (safe concurrency), constraints (integrity), transactions (ACID).
db0-why.analogy: Zip folder vs coded cupboard: In a zip, only files are stored — to search you must open everything, and two users can enter at the same time. Database = a cupboard that contains index cards (instant search), a lock (one person at a time), and a register (everything written follows rules).
db0-why.why: The first "why database?" — the interview answer covers four shortcomings: search, concurrency, integrity, scale. All other topics (index, ACID, replication) are answers to these. Understand the root and the tree builds itself.
gotchas: Just remember: files have four shortcomings — search, concurrency, integrity, scale.
Interview follow-up: "what does indexing do for files?" — indexing.
DBMS vs database: DBMS = software, database = collection of data.
terms: Organized collection of structured data — managed by a DBMS.
Software that stores/queries/updates data — PostgreSQL, MySQL.
A request for data — written in SQL.
Multiple users working on data at the same time without conflict.
where: users, orders, products — all in a DB.
"Why not files?" — most common first Q.
db0-why.visualCap: Files: everything done manually. Database: search, concurrency, and rules built in.
codeSwap: Write conflict? DB locks + transactions handle karta hai.
Write conflict? The DB handles it with locks + transactions.
Files mein aise search karna (slow + error-prone):

db0-table.name: Tables, rows, and columns
db0-table.desc: A table is the fundamental storage unit — like a spreadsheet with a fixed structure. Columns define the structure with names and data types. Rows hold the actual data.
db0-table.q: What is a table? What are columns and rows? How do data types matter?
db0-table.qsub: What is the difference between schema and data? Why does one table model one entity?
db0-table.what:
Table is like a spreadsheet: columns define the structure (which fields, which types), rows contain the data (each row = a record). Schema = layout; data = content. Keeping the difference clear is essential.

A table models a single entity — users table, orders table, products table. Data types give a contract to a column: VARCHAR(50) means up to 50 characters, DECIMAL(10,2) means monetary values. Wrong type = wrong data.
db0-table.analogy: Empty register vs filled register: schema = the empty register's columns (date, name, amount), data = the filled rows. Fix the register format first, then write — that's a table.
db0-table.why: Every SQL query runs on a table. Schema vs data, entity modeling, data types — these are interview basics. "Explain a table like I am 5" works like this: columns = structure, rows = values.
gotchas: Just remember: columns = structure (schema), rows = data, a table = an entity.
NOT NULL vs empty string: an empty string is also a value.
Interview: VARCHAR(50) 50-char limit — set it based on expected data.
terms: Fundamental storage unit — like a spreadsheet with a fixed structure.
Table's structure — name + data type (INT, TEXT, DATE).
A record — values of the columns in one line.
Table layout — which columns, which types.
db0-table.visualCap: Table: columns (structure) × rows (records). A table = an entity.

db0-pk.name: Primary Key — uniquely identifies every row
db0-pk.desc: A Primary Key uniquely identifies each row. It cannot be NULL, no duplicates allowed. Database auto-creates an index on it for fast O(log n) lookups.
db0-pk.q: What is a primary key? What properties must it satisfy?
db0-pk.qsub: What is the difference between a natural key and a surrogate key? When would you use UUID vs auto-increment?
db0-pk.what:
Primary Key (PK) uniquely identifies each row. Rules: cannot be NULL, no duplicates. The DB automatically creates an auto index on it, so WHERE id = 5 is instant (O(log n)).

Surrogate (auto-increment, UUID) vs natural (email, Aadhaar): a surrogate stays under control and never changes. A natural key can change (email changes) — therefore in production prefer a surrogate.
db0-pk.analogy: Roll number: in school each student has a unique roll number — that’s the PK. Names can be the same (two Rahuls), roll numbers cannot. Name = natural key (can change), roll number = surrogate (fixed).
db0-pk.why: Without a PK targeting is impossible — updates/deletes would affect multiple rows. Every relationship (FK) refers to a PK. Classic interview question: "UUID vs auto-increment?" — when data never changes, a natural key can also work.
cons: A natural PK mistakenly used as PK.
gotchas: Just remember: PK = unique + NOT NULL + auto-index; prefer surrogate.
Email as PK? If email changes, every FK must be updated.
Interview: UUID PK can cause index fragmentation — sequential PK is fast.
terms: Unique identifier for each row — no duplicates, no NULL.
Constraint — a value cannot appear more than once.
Artificial key (auto-increment id, UUID) — no real-world meaning.
Key derived from data — like Aadhaar number, email.
DB automatically creates an index on the PK — fast lookup.
db0-pk.visualCap: PK: unique + NOT NULL. DB auto-indexes = fast lookup.
svgSwap: every row in just one place

db0-fk.name: Foreign Key — links rows across tables
db0-fk.desc: A Foreign Key references the Primary Key of another table, creating relationships. Database enforces referential integrity — you cannot create an order for a non-existent user.
db0-fk.q: What is a foreign key? How does it enforce referential integrity?
db0-fk.qsub: What is the difference between ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL? When would you use each?
db0-fk.what:
Foreign Key (FK) is a column that points to another table's PK. It creates relationships: an order belongs to a user, the user_id links to the user. The DB enforces referential integrity — such an order cannot be created without an existing user.

You must set an ON DELETE policy: CASCADE (if the user disappears, orders also disappear) or SET NULL (order remains, user_id becomes NULL). This choice depends on business logic.
db0-fk.analogy: PAN card + jobs list: Aadhaar/PAN card = PK (unique identifier). In the jobs list, the "Aadhaar number" column is an FK — the number written must actually be a valid Aadhaar. If an incorrect number is entered, the register check will reject it — that's referential integrity.
db0-fk.why: FK is the basis of relationships/joins. When merging (interview: inner join) the DB uses FK to know how to join. Integrity ensures data never becomes an "air-hostess with no flight".
gotchas: Just remember: FK = reference to another table's PK; DB enforces integrity.
Use ON DELETE CASCADE carefully — deleting a parent can remove an entire subtree.
Interview: Need to delete all rows quickly? Use TRUNCATE — FK checks are also skipped.
terms: Column that references another table's PK — creates a link.
Rule: FK value must exist in the parent table.
When parent is deleted, child is also deleted.
When parent is deleted, child's reference becomes NULL.
Models an M:N relation using two tables plus a linking table.
db0-fk.visualCap: FK links child → parent PK. Orphan records can never be created.

d2.name: DML — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE patterns
d2.desc: DML operates on row data. SELECT retrieves, INSERT adds, UPDATE modifies, DELETE removes. UPSERT patterns handle duplicate keys. RETURNING clause returns affected rows.
d2.q: What are the DML commands? How does UPSERT work in PostgreSQL vs MySQL?
d2.qsub: When would you use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE vs a separate UPDATE query?
d2.what:
DML works with rows — SELECT (read), INSERT (add), UPDATE (modify), DELETE (remove). DDL works on the schema, DML on data.

Interview and production patterns: UPSERT — first insert, update on duplicate. PostgreSQL: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET .... MySQL: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE. And the RETURNING clause returns affected rows (without an extra SELECT). Bulk inserts (200 rows in a single INSERT) are much faster than row-by-row.
d2.analogy: Diary note: SELECT = read, INSERT = new page, UPDATE = correct a mistake (with an eraser), DELETE = tear out a page. UPSERT = "first check if the name exists; if it does, update the details, otherwise insert". RETURNING = after the change, "how many rows were affected?" say it immediately.
d2.why: Interview warm-up questions start here — insert/update/delete with correct syntax, upsert pattern. This skill is needed for everyday backend work. "How do you handle duplicate inserts?" — the upsert answer is a strong signal.
cons: Bulk operations incur FK check cost.
gotchas: Just remember: UPSERT = insert + update in one; RETURNING = affected rows without an extra query.
ON CONFLICT requires a unique constraint or index on the target.
Interview: bulk 1,000 rows in a single transaction — always disable autocommit.
terms: Data Manipulation Language — works on rows: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
Insert, and if a duplicate occurs then update — ON CONFLICT (PostgreSQL), ON DUPLICATE KEY (MySQL).
Multi-row INSERT or many rows in one go.
COPY / multi-values — 100× faster than single-row inserts.
d2.visualCap: DML on rows: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE + UPSERT & RETURNING patterns.
codeSwap: Upsert (PostgreSQL): email pehle se hai to update
Upsert (PostgreSQL): update if the email already exists

d3.name: SELECT execution order
d3.desc: SQL does not run top-to-bottom. Fixed logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Aliases defined in SELECT are not available in WHERE.
d3.q: What is the logical execution order of a SQL SELECT query?
d3.qsub: Why can you not use a column alias from SELECT in a WHERE clause? In which clauses can you use aliases?
d3.what:
SQL visually appears top-to-bottom but logically runs in a different order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.

Understanding this is critical: aliases are created in SELECT — therefore WHERE cannot use them (WHERE runs earlier), ORDER BY can (later). Filters (WHERE) reduce rows first, then grouping, then HAVING filters groups.
d3.analogy: Cooking line: first take ingredients from the pantry (FROM) → remove bad ingredients (WHERE) → make containers (GROUP BY) → clean containers (HAVING) → decide what to serve (SELECT) → arrange on plates (ORDER BY) → show only 5 guests (LIMIT). The sale justification protocol: next yogurt here.
d3.why: "Why can't I use an alias in WHERE?" — the most asked SQL question. Having the execution order framework clarifies set-logic and query rewriting. Explain to the interviewer step by step.
cons: Visual vs logical order can be confusing.
gotchas: Just remember: FROM WHERE GROUP HAVING SELECT ORDER LIMIT; alias not allowed in WHERE.
DISTINCT is applied after SELECT — therefore ORDER BY is allowed on columns not in the SELECT list.
Interview: GROUP BY column must also be in the SELECT list — strict databases require it.
terms: SQL's actual execution sequence — starts with FROM, ends with LIMIT.
Table(s) source — creates the initial working set.
After grouping, HAVING filters the groups.
Removes duplicates — after SELECT, before ORDER.
SELECT aliases are available only in SELECT/ORDER BY; not in WHERE/GROUP BY.
d3.visualCap: 6-step pipeline: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER → LIMIT.

sql2.name: JOINs — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL, CROSS, SELF
sql2.desc: JOINs combine rows from multiple tables based on related columns. INNER JOIN returns only matching rows. LEFT JOIN returns all left rows with NULLs for missing matches. Self-join joins a table with itself.
sql2.q: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN? When would you use each?
sql2.qsub: What is a self-join? How do you find employees and their managers from the same table?
sql2.what:
JOIN connects rows from different tables on a related column. INNER = only rows that match in both. LEFT = all left rows plus matching right rows, missing become NULL. RIGHT is the opposite. FULL = all rows from both sides. CROSS = every combination (without a condition). SELF = same table joined twice with aliases.

Classic example: in an employees table the manager column always holds an employee id — JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id. A favorite interview question.
sql2.analogy: Friend list merge: INNER = those present in both lists; LEFT = all from your list, and if not in the other list the box is empty (NULL); FULL = the total unique people from both lists, with blanks where the other side is missing. SELF = compare the same list as "boss" and "junior".
sql2.why: JOINs are the superpower of relational databases. About 80% of interview query questions involve joins. The difference between INNER and LEFT is NULL handling — whenever you need all left-side rows (including those without a match), use LEFT JOIN.
gotchas: Just remember: INNER = overlap; LEFT = all left + NULL; RIGHT = opposite; FULL = all.
JOIN occurs before WHERE: put filters in the ON condition or in WHERE — both affect result type, but performance differs.
Interview: if you see duplicate rows, check the ON condition (it may have become 1:N).
terms: Only matching pairs — present in both tables.
All rows from left table plus matching right rows (otherwise NULL).
All rows from right table plus matching left rows.
All rows from both sides, missing side NULL (combined).
Every left row × every right row — Cartesian.
Joining a table to itself — like manager-employee.
sql2.visualCap: Venn: INNER = overlap, LEFT = left all, FULL = all all.

sql3.name: Aggregation — COUNT, SUM, AVG, GROUP BY, HAVING
sql3.desc: GROUP BY collapses many rows into one per unique value. Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) calculate per group. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, unlike WHERE which filters before.
sql3.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING? When do you use each?
sql3.qsub: Why does COUNT(*) count all rows but COUNT(column) exclude NULLs? What is the difference?
sql3.what:
Aggregates turn many rows into a single value. COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. GROUP BY splits rows into groups and runs an aggregate on each group — GROUP BY dept + COUNT(*) = count per department.

HAVING filters groups (after aggregation), WHERE filters rows before grouping. COUNT(*) counts all rows, COUNT(col) skips NULLs. Remember: selecting a non-grouped column together with an aggregate is an error.
sql3.analogy: Scoreboard in groups: GROUP BY creates teams (team = login); SUM = total score per team; HAVING = show only teams whose total > 100. WHERE first removes players who cannot play; HAVING then filters teams.
sql3.why: Aggregation is the heart of analytics queries. "dept-wise count", "avg salary per city" — core of every interview SQL round. WHERE vs HAVING is a one-line difference: rows vs groups.
gotchas: Just remember: WHERE before rows, HAVING after groups; COUNT(*) all, COUNT(col) skips NULL.
Interview: when using aggregates, select only grouped/GROUP BY columns.
DISTINCT COUNT: COUNT(DISTINCT city) — unique cities.
terms: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX — many rows → one number.
Grouping rows — an aggregate per group.
COUNT(*) counts all rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs.
sql3.visualCap: Rows → GROUP BY (teams) → HAVING (team filter). AVG per group.

db0-select.name: Your first query — SELECT
db0-select.desc: SELECT is how you read data. SELECT * returns all columns. SELECT name, email returns specific columns. SQL execution order: FROM → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
db0-select.q: How does SELECT work? What is the order of SQL clause execution?
db0-select.qsub: Why can you not use a column alias defined in SELECT inside a WHERE clause?
db0-select.what:
SELECT is the mantra for reading data. SELECT * FROM users = all columns, SELECT name, email = only those columns (projection). You can give an AS alias — the output name changes.

Supreme rule: SQL does not run top-to-bottom. Logical order: FROM (which table) → WHERE (filter) → SELECT (project) → ORDER BY (sort) → LIMIT. That’s why an alias defined in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE — the alias does not exist yet.
db0-select.analogy: Going to a market: first decide the vendor (shop/FROM), then sift (filter/WHERE), then pick the amount you need (SELECT), then arrange in line (ORDER), then take only 10 (LIMIT). The order is everything.
db0-select.why: The foundation of every interview SQL question is the execution order. The answer to “Why can’t an alias be used in WHERE?” is right here. SELECT is not just for display — it truly performs projection and calculations after filtering.
cons: ORDER BY can be slow on big data.
gotchas: Just remember: FROM → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT; alias cannot be used in WHERE.
Avoid SELECT * in production — unnecessary columns and it breaks index-only scans.
Interview: alias works in ORDER BY but not in WHERE.
terms: Data reading command — * means all columns.
Which columns to show — SELECT name, email.
Temporary name for a column/table — AS.
FROM → WHERE → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT (logical).
db0-select.visualCap: Logical execution: FROM first, LIMIT last. Alias is created according to that order.
codeSwap: Note: the 'name' alias isn't in WHERE,
SELECT id, name AS naam, email
SELECT id, name AS full_name, email

db0-where.name: Filtering rows — WHERE, AND, OR, NOT
db0-where.desc: WHERE filters which rows are returned. Supports comparisons (=, !=, <, >), logical operators (AND, OR, NOT), pattern matching (LIKE), set membership (IN), range (BETWEEN), and null checks.
db0-where.q: How does WHERE filter rows? What operators does it support?
db0-where.qsub: Why does WHERE email = NULL not work? What should you use instead?
db0-where.what:
WHERE filters rows. Operators: =, !=, <, >, LIKE (pattern), IN (membership), BETWEEN (range), IS NULL (null check), and combine with AND/OR/NOT.

Classic trap: WHERE email = NULL never works — NULL is not a value, it means “unknown”. Use IS NULL. AND means both, OR means either — use parentheses to make precedence clear.
db0-where.analogy: Screening machine (security): if the check fails → side. AND = "ID check AND bag check" (both required), OR = "talk to manager OR authorized card" (either is enough). NULL = the exam was not cleared at all (use IS NULL check).
db0-where.why: The less data that reaches WHERE, the faster the query. Filtering happens on the result set. A favorite interview edge: NULL comparison, LIKE wildcards, and predicate push.
gotchas: Just remember: NULL cannot be compared with =; use IS NULL; AND = both, OR = either.
LIKE 'A%' can use an index; LIKE '%A' cannot (leading wildcard).
Interview: NOT IN (NULL) always returns empty — because of NULL’s three-value logic.
terms: Row filter — only rows where the condition matches proceed.
db0-where.visualCap: WHERE filters: AND = both true, OR = either true, NOT = opposite.
codeSwap: GLTI: WHERE email = NULL;  -- kabhi fail nahi hoga
WRONG: WHERE email = NULL;  -- never matches

db0-crud.name: Basic CRUD — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
db0-crud.desc: CRUD = Create, Read, Update, Delete. INSERT INTO creates rows, SELECT reads, UPDATE modifies, DELETE removes. Always use WHERE with UPDATE/DELETE or you affect every row.
db0-crud.q: What are the four CRUD operations? Why must you always use WHERE with UPDATE and DELETE?
db0-crud.qsub: What is a soft delete pattern? Why is it preferred over hard deletes in production?
db0-crud.what:
CRUD = the four operations on a dataset: INSERT (create), SELECT (read), UPDATE (update), DELETE (delete). No application runs without them.

Golden rule: UPDATE / DELETE must always have a WHERE — otherwise the entire table will have its values changed or rows deleted. In production, soft delete is preferred: set a deleted_at column, which provides data history and restore capability. Hard delete is used only where privacy or regulations (e.g., KYC) require it.
db0-crud.analogy: Register entry: INSERT = write a new name; SELECT = read who is there; UPDATE = add "married" next to a name; DELETE = tear out the page (hard!) vs soft = keep the page and mark the name with a ✗. Any audit prefers the marked-option.
db0-crud.why: Interview prompt “write CRUD for a user” tests basic competency. The real trick is UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE (a bug) and the soft-delete pattern. It shows production experience, and often leads to a follow-up “why soft delete?”
gotchas: Just remember: UPDATE/DELETE always with WHERE; soft delete = deleted_at flag.
After soft delete, SELECT queries must also filter with deleted_at IS NULL.
Interview: TRUNCATE is different from DELETE — it removes the whole table quickly, but foreign-key constraints cause delays.
terms: Flag instead of DELETE — deleted_at timestamp; data is retained.
db0-crud.visualCap: CRUD: Insert → Select → Update → Delete. Always WHERE with UPDATE/DELETE.
codeSwap: Update (WHERE bhoola to SAB badal jayega!)

d1.name: DDL — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
d1.desc: DDL defines database schema. CREATE TABLE with column types and constraints (PK, FK, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT). ALTER TABLE for modifications. DROP removes objects entirely.
d1.q: What are the DDL commands? How do constraints like CHECK and UNIQUE work?
d1.qsub: What is the difference between TRUNCATE and DELETE? Why can TRUNCATE not be rolled back in some databases?
d1.what:
DDL = commands that define the schema. CREATE TABLE creates a new table with column types and constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK, DEFAULT, NOT NULL). ALTER TABLE adds, removes, drops columns and changes constraints. DROP removes the entire table (data + structure).

TRUNCATE vs DELETE — important to understand: DELETE removes rows conditionally (WHERE), participates in transactions, is slow (row-by-row), and fires triggers. TRUNCATE is instant, removes all table data, and in many databases cannot be rolled back and fails on foreign keys. For production demo queries, TRUNCATE is preferable.
d1.analogy: Building contractors: CREATE = lay a new foundation and floors. ALTER = rename/remove a floor, add a new window. DROP = take down the entire building (empty lot). TRUNCATE = the building remains but all interior fittings are removed — the space is empty.
d1.why: Schema design is a top interview topic: “what are constraints?” and “TRUNCATE vs DELETE?” — precise answers come from here. Knowing the correct way to handle migrations (ALTER) is essential for a production career.
gotchas: Just remember: TRUNCATE = data gone, table remains; DROP = table gone; ALTER = changes.
MySQL TRUNCATE resets the auto-increment counter.
Interview: CHECK (price >= 0) constraint — only valid data can be entered.
terms: Data Definition Language — creates/changes schema: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE.
New table with columns and constraints.
Completely remove an object — the table is gone.
Remove all DATA from a table, keep the structure.
d1.visualCap: TRUNCATE = remove data, keep structure. DROP = everything.

sql4.name: Subqueries & CTEs
sql4.desc: Subqueries are queries inside other queries. CTEs (WITH keyword) give subqueries a name for readability. Correlated subqueries reference outer query columns and execute row-by-row.
sql4.q: What is the difference between a correlated subquery and a regular subquery?
sql4.qsub: Why is EXISTS typically faster than IN for large subquery result sets?
sql4.what:
Subquery = a query inside another query. CTE (WITH x AS (...)) gives the subquery a name — readable, reusable. Correlated subquery references outer rows, so it can run for each outer row.

In an inline filter, EXISTS is often faster than IN — EXISTS stops as soon as a matching row is found, while IN builds the entire list and compares. As soon as a match is found in the subquery, it stops.
sql4.analogy: Internal exam marks in a form: subquery = "first retrieve the marks, then the main query uses them". CTE = give that result a name like "MarksReport" — reusable later. Correlated = for each student, separately check the marks section (one by one).
sql4.why: Modular query building — complex features (top-per-group, filtering by aggregate) come from here. CTE improves readability and performance; interviewers want to see that you break complex logic into simple components.
gotchas: Just remember: CTE = named subquery; EXISTS early-stops; correlated runs on each row.
Interview: CTE struggles with nested subqueries — readability + testability.
Recursive CTE can only be created with WITH.
terms: A query inside a query — in parentheses.
WITH clause — gives the subquery a name and re-use.
References columns from the outer query; runs on each row.
Existence check — does the subquery return a row? Stops immediately.
IN = list membership; EXISTS = existence check, often fast.
sql4.visualCap: Subquery = inner query; CTE = named subquery (WITH). Correlated = per-row.

d7.name: Set operations — UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
d7.desc: Set operations combine results from multiple SELECTs. UNION merges without duplicates (requires sort). UNION ALL concatenates with duplicates (faster). INTERSECT returns common rows. EXCEPT returns rows in first but not second.
d7.q: What is the difference between UNION and UNION ALL? When would you use each?
d7.qsub: How would you find customers who bought product A but NOT product B?
d7.what:
Set operations combine result sets: UNION (deduplicate common rows), UNION ALL (keep all), INTERSECT (common), EXCEPT (rows in the first set but not the second). Columns count/types must be the same.

UNION vs UNION ALL: UNION performs sort/dedup to remove duplicates = slower; UNION ALL simply concatenates = faster. When you know there are no duplicates, use UNION ALL. Classic interview: "customers who bought A but not B" → SELECT ... EXCEPT SELECT ....
d7.analogy: Two class student lists: UNION = combine and keep unique names (each name appears once even if in both). UNION ALL = write all names; names appearing in both appear twice. INTERSECT = names present in both lists. EXCEPT = students in class A who are not in class B.
d7.why: Multi-condition queries (like "either this or that data") become clean with set ops. UNION for dedup vs UNION ALL for performance — a common interview point. INTERSECT/EXCEPT are simple diff tool queries.
gotchas: Just remember: UNION dedups (slow), UNION ALL concatenates (fast), INTERSECT common, EXCEPT A minus B.
ORDER BY/LIMIT applies to the whole UNION — after the last SELECT.
Interview: columns count/types must be the same otherwise error.
terms: Join result sets vertically — remove duplicates.
Combine all — keep duplicates, fast (no sort).
In the first set but not the second.
d7.visualCap: UNION = dedup combine; UNION ALL = all; INTERSECT = common; EXCEPT = only A.

si1.name: What is an Index? — when to add one, B-tree vs hash (concept)
si1.desc: An index is a data structure that speeds up row lookups at the cost of slower writes. Without an index, the database scans every row (sequential scan). With an index, it jumps directly to the matching rows. Think of a book index — instead of reading every page, you look up the topic and go straight there.
si1.q: What is a database index? When should you add one and when should you not?
si1.qsub: What is the difference between a B-tree index and a hash index? When would you use each? What happens to write performance when you add too many indexes?
si1.what:
Index = a book index. Without it the DB scans every row (sequential scan — read everything). With an index the DB jumps directly to matching rows. Most databases default to B-tree (sorted tree) — works for equality and range queries.

But nothing is free: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE also updates the index — writes become slower. Too many indexes = more storage + slower writes. Balance: add indexes for hot queries; keep few on write-heavy small tables.
si1.analogy: Library without an index: to find a book you have to scan every shelf (sequential scan). With a card catalogue (index): "Sharma, R — shelf 3, row 4" — go directly. But each new book requires a catalogue card update (write cost).
si1.why: Timing: index is the #1 database interview topic. "Why index?" → categorization. "When to add?" → read-heavy + WHERE-predicate columns. B-tree vs hash — different access patterns. Performance = query planning aided by indexes.
gotchas: Just remember: index = book index; reads fast, writes slow; B-tree default.
Selectivity matters: an index on a column with only 2 distinct values will perform poorly.
Interview: expression indexes (e.g., lower(email)) — the column inside a function is not indexed.
terms: Data structure that makes lookups fast — like a book index.
Without index — read every row (slow on large table).
Sorted tree — supports both range and equality.
Every insert/update also updates the index — writes slow.
si1.visualCap: Without index: scan all rows. With index: jump straight to target.

si1b.name: B-Tree & B+Tree — structure, fanout, range scans
si1b.desc: B+ Trees are the default index in most databases. Self-balancing trees with data only in leaf nodes, which are linked for fast range scans. Height is 3-4 for billions of rows — very few disk seeks.
si1b.q: How does a B+ Tree index work? Why is it efficient for both lookups and range scans?
si1b.qsub: What is the difference between B-Tree and B+ Tree? Why do databases prefer B+ Tree?
si1b.what:
B+ Tree is the default index in relational databases. Data resides only in leaf nodes, internal nodes contain only keys (guides). Leaves are connected via a linked list, so range scans (e.g., [1,10]) are easy — move from one leaf to the next. A large fanout keeps the tree height low — even with 1 billion rows you need only 3-4 disk seeks.

B-Tree stores data in every node — point lookups work, but range scans require moving back up to parent nodes (slow). Hence B+ Tree is the database favorite.
si1b.analogy: Railway division maps: each zone corresponds to an internal node (route map), the actual stations (data) are on leaf nodes. Zones are linked, so traveling from "station 5 to 15" can be done by walking leaf-to-leaf without backtracking. Two maps: data on all pages (B-tree) vs only station pages (B+).
si1b.why: Index interview core — why B+ Tree, what fanout is, why range is fast. Disk I/O = seeks; a small height means few seeks. Explaining this signals senior-level knowledge.
cons: Point lookup on hash is slower compared.
gotchas: Just remember: data only in leaves, leaves linked; height 3-4 even on billions; B+ wins for range.
Interview: large B+ fanout = flat tree, fewer disk reads.
Without the leading column of a composite index — B+ cannot use it.
terms: Default index — sorted tree; data only in leaves, leaves linked.
Number of children per node — larger = smaller tree.
Leaf linked list walk forward/backward — fast.
Levels from root to leaf — 3-4 on billions of rows.
B-tree: data in every node. B+: data only in leaves. B+ provides better range scans.
si1b.visualCap: Internal nodes = keys only; leaves = data, linked → fast range scan.

si2.name: LSM-Tree — memtable, SSTable, compaction
si2.desc: LSM-Trees make writes super fast by writing to memory first (memtable), then flushing sorted files (SSTables) to disk. Background compaction merges SSTables. Trade-off: reads check multiple files.
si2.q: How does an LSM-Tree optimize write performance? What is the write path?
si2.qsub: What is the difference between size-tiered and leveled compaction? How do bloom filters help LSM reads?
si2.what:
LSM-Tree (Log-Structured Merge) makes writes ultra-fast. Write path: first the memtable (sorted in RAM) — instant acknowledgment. As soon as it fills, the SSTable (sorted file) is flushed to disk. Background compaction merges small files into larger sorted files.

The cost of reads: a key may reside in many files — therefore Bloom filters indicate whether a file might contain the key. This avoids checking all files. Trade-offs: size-tiered (merge only same-size files) vs leveled (level-by-level, cleaner). This is the engine behind Cassandra, RocksDB, SQLite-WAL.
si2.analogy: Small notebook analogy: write the data immediately on a clean parchment (memtable/RAM), no waiting (fast ack). When the paper fills, it is written to sealed files (SSTables). In the evening, all files are gathered and cleaned (compaction). When searching, look at RAM (memtable) first, then files, and the bloom filter tells whether a particular file needs to be examined.
si2.why: Write-heavy systems (Cassandra, RocksDB, DynamoDB) use LSM — a common interview deep-dive topic. The B-tree vs LSM trade-off: B-tree offers fast reads but costly writes; LSM makes writes cheap. "Why are Kafka-style appends ultra fast?" — this is the same logic.
gotchas: Just remember: memtable → SSTable → compaction; writes are fast, reads pay with bloom.
Interview: Are large reads in LSM like Google? No — point reads are fine, aggregate scans are costly.
Compaction storms can cause peak-hour I/O spikes.
terms: Write-optimized structure — memory first, then sorted files.
Sorted collection in RAM — writes go here.
Sorted string table — sorted file on disk.
Indicates whether a file may contain a key — speeds reads.
si2.visualCap: LSM write path: memtable(RAM) → SSTable(disk) → compaction merge.

si6.name: Buffer pool — LRU, dirty pages, checkpoints
si6.desc: The buffer pool is the database RAM cache. Reads check memory first (cache hit = instant). On miss, reads from disk, stores in pool. When full, evicts least recently used page. Target: 95%+ hit rate.
si6.q: What is a buffer pool? How does it improve database performance?
si6.qsub: What are dirty pages? What is a checkpoint and why does it cause I/O spikes?
si6.what:
Buffer pool is the database’s RAM cache. Every read looks in RAM first (hit = instant, miss = disk). When full, the least-used allocation (LRU) evicts a page.

Dirty pages are pages that have been modified in RAM but not written to disk — they must be persisted after a crash. A checkpoint forces dirty pages to be written to disk so that crash recovery is short. Target: 95%+ hit rate — below that means less RAM and higher I/O cost.
si6.analogy: Kitchen counter + fridge: frequently used items are on the counter (buffer pool) — instantly available. Infrequent items come from the fridge (disk). When the counter fills, the oldest items are moved to the fridge (LRU). "The dish is on the counter but the recipe changed" = dirty page — you clean it at night (checkpoint) so the next morning the entry is clean.
si6.why: Disk I/O is the slowest component. The higher the buffer-pool hit rate, the faster the DB. Interview topics include cache-hit-ratio metrics, dirty pages/checkpoint and I/O spikes — signals for production operation. This also explains why databases run primarily in "memory".
gotchas: Just remember: buffer pool = RAM cache; hit rate 95%+; dirty pages → checkpoint.
A large checkpoint interval makes recovery slow (long replay).
Interview: LRU is not "random eviction" — it provides predictability.
terms: DB’s RAM cache — pages are kept in memory.
Page found in RAM — no disk read.
Modified in RAM but not yet written to disk.
Least Recently Used — evict the least used page.
Force dirty pages to disk — ensures durability.
si6.visualCap: Read: RAM first (hit) → disk (miss). Dirty pages → checkpoint flush.
codeSwap: > 0.95 = good. Change kam to RAM/system tune.

si3.name: Hash indexes — O(1) point lookups
si3.desc: Hash indexes map keys to disk locations via hash function — instant O(1) exact-match lookups. Cannot support range queries because hashing scrambles order. Good for WHERE email = x.
si3.q: When would you use a hash index instead of a B-Tree index?
si3.qsub: What is extendible hashing? How does it handle bucket overflow gracefully?
si3.what:
Hash index maps a key to a bucket using a hash function — exact match WHERE email = x is O(1). Unlike a B-tree, there is no log(n) walk — just one jump. However, range queries (BETWEEN) are impossible because hashing destroys order.

Extendible hashing handles bucket overflow: a bucket splits and the directory (pointer list) grows. In practice hash indexes are rare (PostgreSQL hashm access method), but the concept shows why exact-match lookups are fast.
si3.analogy: Locker index: compute the first letter of a name and go directly to the locker block (hash) — one step, limited. But "all people whose names are between R and T" (range) cannot be retrieved because lockers are not ordered by hash. A book index (B-tree) handles that.
si3.why: Interview: "hash vs B-tree index?" — use cases: equality-heavy (cache, KV lookups) vs range. This also illustrates that every data structure has its own trade-offs.
gotchas: Just remember: hash = O(1) exact match; range = B-tree domain.
Interview: PostgreSQL hash index is now WAL-safe (PG 10+).
Hash collisions mean a bucket can become small, but still work — therefore B-tree remains the default.
terms: Key hash → bucket location — exact match O(1).
Keys that collide share the same bucket.
Buckets split when overflow — directory pointers grow.
Hash supports only =, B-tree supports range and =.
Compute a hash, go to one location — fast point read.
si3.visualCap: Hash index: key → O(1) bucket. Exact match fast, range not possible.

si5.name: Bitmap indexes — low-cardinality columns
si5.desc: Bitmap indexes store a bit array per distinct value — each bit says if a row has that value. ANDing bitmaps finds intersections instantly. Only useful for columns with few distinct values (status, region).
si5.q: What is a bitmap index? When is it useful and when is it not?
si5.qsub: How do you combine multiple bitmap indexes for complex boolean queries?
si5.what:
Bitmap index stores a bit array for each distinct value: the i-th bit is 1 if row i contains that value. WHERE status = 'active' AND tier = 'gold' → AND the two bitmaps with a AND — a CPU bitwise operation that yields an immediate result. Therefore it works well for low-cardinality columns (status, region, gender).

For high-cardinality columns (email, timestamp) the bitmap becomes large because each value needs its own array. It is popular in data warehouses (OLAP) and rare in OLTP.
si5.analogy: 400-person language register: each person gets a bit. "Who is from Delhi?" = one column with 1s. "Industry tech AND Delhi" = AND of two columns — fast. But if every person has a unique city, you would need a separate column for each city — thousands of columns — wasteful.
si5.why: It comes up in OLAP/columnar discussions — "how does a warehouse filter quickly on low-cardinality?" Bitmap AND shows the answer. It also serves as an example of "when NOT to index".
gotchas: Just remember: bitmap = per-value bit-array; king of low-cardinality; AND gives instant results.
Interview: bitmap updates are difficult — writes are expensive (page lock).
COUNT queries are also fast with a bitmap — just count the 1s.
terms: Bit array for each distinct value — 1 means the row has that value.
Few distinct values (status, gender) — bitmap excels.
Intersection of two bitmaps — instant AND on the index.
Many distinct values (email) — bitmap becomes large.
si5.visualCap: Bitmap: value per bit-array. AND two bitmaps = instant filter.

sql12.name: Views & Materialized Views
sql12.desc: Views are saved queries — virtual tables for readability and security. Materialized Views store actual results on disk for fast reads but data goes stale. Must REFRESH to update.
sql12.q: What is the difference between a regular view and a materialized view?
sql12.qsub: When would you use a materialized view instead of a regular view? What are the staleness trade-offs?
sql12.what:
View = a saved query that appears like a table. Every SELECT runs the query again — a live picture of new data. Use: hide complexity, provide consistent interface, security (only some columns).

Materialized View stores the result on disk — reads are instant (full query not executed), but data is stale — update with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW. Use: expensive aggregations, reporting where slight delay is acceptable.
sql12.analogy: Live recording vs photograph: View = live camera feed — shows the real state whenever you look. Materialized view = printed photo — appears instantly but remains the same even after changes; a new photo (REFRESH) must be taken. Reports = prints, dashboards = live.
sql12.why: Interview: "view vs materialized view" — one-line diff: live query vs cached snapshot. This is also an example of read-optimization without saying it. Mentioning the staleness trade-off shows production awareness.
gotchas: Remember: view = live saved query; materialized view = cached snapshot + REFRESH.
Interview: materialized view can have indexes — reads become fast.
Updatable views are limited (PostgreSQL) — only simple queries.
terms: Saved query — virtual table; does not store data, runs each time.
Query result stored on disk — fast reads, but stale.
Updates the materialized view (manual or scheduled).
View can hide columns — also row-level.
Materialized view data lags behind its source — waiting for REFRESH.
sql12.visualCap: View = live query. Materialized view = stored snapshot + REFRESH.

sql13.name: Stored Procedures, Functions, Triggers
sql13.desc: Stored Procedures are saved SQL code blocks with parameters and logic. Functions return a value and can be used in SELECT. Triggers fire automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE events.
sql13.q: What is the difference between a stored procedure and a function?
sql13.qsub: When should you use triggers? What problems can overusing triggers cause?
sql13.what:
Stored Procedures = saved block of SQL+logic that resides on the server. Functions return a value (scalar or tabular) — SELECT my_func(x). Triggers automatically fire on table events — used for logging, denormalization, audit.

Interview short diff: procedure is an action/sequence; function is a value; trigger runs automatically. Overusing triggers leads to hidden magic that callers are unaware of, creating debugging hell.
sql13.analogy: Restaurant recipe cards (available to the app): procedure = "a detailed tray — 10 steps, dish ready" (call: CALL make_biryani). Function = "is this price valid?" (SELECT is_valid()). Trigger = "as soon as an order arrives, print the bill" — you don’t ask, the system does it. But many triggers become "ghost waiters", hard to understand.
sql13.why: Interview: "procedure vs function", "why avoid triggers?" — placement of data-bound logic. This also appears in legacy systems’ code. Auditing/denormalization through triggers is a common pattern.
gotchas: Remember: proc = action; func = value; trigger = auto-fire; be careful with triggers.
Trigger recursion: trigger → insert → trigger... cycles.
Interview: stored logic is harder to test than application logic.
terms: Saved SQL code block — logic, params, return multiple results.
Returns a value — can be used in SELECT.
Runs with the permission of the procedure owner — be careful.
sql13.visualCap: Procedure = action block; Function = returns value; Trigger = auto-fire on event.

e7.name: Table partitioning — Range, List, Hash
e7.desc: Partitioning splits a huge table into smaller pieces while it looks like one table. Range by date, List by discrete values, Hash for even distribution. Partition pruning skips irrelevant partitions.
e7.q: What is partition pruning? How does it improve query performance?
e7.qsub: When would you drop a partition instead of using DELETE? What are the trade-offs?
e7.what:
Partitioning breaks a large table into smaller physical segments (logically still one table). Types: Range (date bins), List (discrete values), Hash (even spread).

Partition pruning magic: the query scans only the partitions that are needed — WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01' skips many partitions. Dropping old data: DROP PARTITION instead of DELETE (avoids full-table scan). Provides both retention and performance.
e7.analogy: Museum’s year-based storage rooms: the whole museum is one (logical), but 2024 items are in the 2024 room (partition). “Show 2024 items” = open only that room (pruning). Removing old items = not emptying the whole museum, just closing one room’s door (DROP PARTITION).
e7.why: Interview: massive tables — partition + pruning. “How to optimize logs?” Range partition (by dates) — common answer. Drop partition vs DELETE (no transaction overhead, less bloat). Practical answer for big-table maintenance.
gotchas: Remember: partition = break it up; pruning = check only what's needed; drop = fast.
Interview: if the WHERE clause lacks the partition key, a full scan will occur.
PostgreSQL requires an index on each partition (inherited).
terms: Breaking a large table into smaller physical pieces — logically still one table.
Distribute by hash — even spread, range queries suffer.
Optimizer accesses only relevant partitions — faster, less I/O.
e7.visualCap: One logical table, physical partitions. Query → pruning → only needed part.

e8.name: Full-text search — inverted indexes
e8.desc: Full-text search finds words inside text much smarter than LIKE. Uses inverted index: for each word, stores list of documents containing it. Handles stemming, stop words, and relevance ranking.
e8.q: How does an inverted index power full-text search?
e8.qsub: What is the difference between tsvector and tsquery in PostgreSQL full-text search?
e8.what:
Full-text search is smarter than my LIKE '%word%'. Core: inverted index — for each word, stores the list of documents containing it (like a book index).

In PostgreSQL: to_tsvector processes text into tokens + stemming and removes stop words; to_tsquery builds the search query; @@ matches; ts_rank sorts by relevance. LIKE with a leading % cannot use an inverted index — results in a table scan.
e8.analogy: Huge reverse dictionary: LIKE = "search every page for this word" (slow). FTS = "word → which pages contain it" card — instantly shows where the word appears (inverted). Modern search boxes use this engine — with stemming, "dogs" → "dog".
e8.why: Search-text queries — products, blogs, logs — are solved by FTS. LIKE with a leading wildcard is slow. Interview: "how do full-text indexes work?" → inverted index, stemming. Feature matrix is simple.
gotchas: Remember: inverted = word→docs; tsvector = processed text; @@ matches; LIKE %x% slow.
Interview: LIKE '%x%' does not use an index; LIKE 'x%' does.
Elasticsearch = the same idea at scale.
terms: Word → list of documents — LIKE vice versa.
Search query object — combined with @<> symbols.
e8.visualCap: Inverted index: word → doc list. tsvector/tsquery → @@ match.

sql8.name: Window functions — ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK
sql8.desc: Window functions calculate across related rows without collapsing them like GROUP BY. ROW_NUMBER gives unique numbers. RANK gives ties the same number with gaps. DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps.
sql8.q: What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK?
sql8.qsub: Why can you not use a window function directly in a WHERE clause? How do you filter on window function results?
sql8.what:
Window functions calculate each row relative to its window (related rows) — and rows do not collapse (unlike GROUP BY). OVER() defines the window, PARTITION BY groups (e.g., per department), ORDER BY sets the sequence.

ROW_NUMBER = unique numbers (1,2,3). RANK = ties get the same rank with gaps: 1,1,3. DENSE_RANK = ties get the same rank without gaps: 1,1,2. Classic: “top-3 per department” — rank with a window then filter (subquery).
sql8.analogy: In a runners' race, imagine a plate: ROW_NUMBER = give everyone a ticket (1,2,3,4). RANK = when two runners finish at the same time (tie) both get 2, and the next gets 4 (gap). DENSE_RANK = both get 2, next gets 3 (no gap, all positions correct). For the podium — if you only need the top 3, extract them with a window.
sql8.why: GROUP BY collapses rows into a single line; a window keeps each original row and can provide per-group rankings. “Top-N per group”, “running totals”, “moving average” — window is the solution. Interview questions on this topic go 2–3 levels deep.
cons: Cannot be used directly in WHERE.
gotchas: Just remember: ROW_NUMBER unique; RANK ties+gap; DENSE_RANK ties+no-gap.
Interview: window functions cannot be used in WHERE — therefore wrap with a subquery.
SUM(score) OVER (ORDER BY id) = running total.
terms: For each row, calculation is performed on its "window" (neighbor rows) — rows do not collapse (unlike GROUP BY).
Assigns a unique number to each row — no two are the same.
Ties receive the same rank with gaps: 1,1,3.
Ties receive the same rank without gaps: 1,1,2.

sql10.name: Recursive CTEs — tree/graph traversal
sql10.desc: Recursive CTEs call themselves — perfect for hierarchical data like org charts. Has an anchor member (starting row) and recursive step (joins back to CTE). Runs until no new rows are produced.
sql10.q: How does a recursive CTE work? What are the anchor and recursive members?
sql10.qsub: How would you find all ancestors in a tree? What prevents infinite loops in recursive CTEs?
sql10.what:
A Recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) is a query that refers to itself — perfect for hierarchical data (org chart, category tree, graph). It has two members:

1) Anchor — the starting rows (like the top manager). 2) Recursive member — joins the anchor's results with the CTE to get the next level. This continues until no new row is produced (termination). If there's no de-duplication on each round, is the loop infinite? Careful: cycles can sneak in — keep a visited/level column.
sql10.analogy: Family tree search: start with the ancestor (anchor). “Who is this person's manager” = recursive step — keep finding each person's manager. When the chain ends (no manager) you stop. A cycle (X's manager is Y, Y's manager is X) would cause a loop: keep a “seen list.”
sql10.why: In interviews, tree/graph problems (e.g., full manager chain) are solved with a recursive CTE as a one-line SQL solution. This shows understanding of graph traversal — “find all ancestors” is a common question.
gotchas: Just remember: anchor + recursive member + UNION ALL; stops when no new row is produced.
Interview: to avoid infinite loops, use a level limit or a visited list.
CTE does not automatically drop cycles — it will loop directly.
terms: WITH RECURSIVE — the CTE calls itself.
Joins the CTE to produce the next layer — traverses the tree/chart.
Stops when no new row is produced.
Depth — each iteration increments level by 1.
sql10.visualCap: Recursive CTE: anchor (root) → expand level by level until no new rows.

e3.name: Indexes — B-Tree, Hash, Composite, Covering
e3.desc: Indexes accelerate data access. B-Tree for range and equality. Composite index on (a,b,c) follows leftmost prefix rule. Covering index includes all columns needed — no table lookup required.
e3.q: What is the leftmost prefix rule for composite indexes? Give an example.
e3.qsub: What is a covering index? How does it eliminate key lookups entirely?
e3.what:
Composite index = an index on multiple columns (a,b,c). Queries must follow the leftmost prefix: a, a,b, a,b,c can use the index, but WHERE b = 1 or c = 2 alone will miss the index.

Covering index is an index that contains all columns needed by the query — no need to go to the table (index-only scan), reads are ultra fast. Trade-off: the larger the index, the more storage and write overhead.
e3.analogy: Phone book (last_name, first_name) sorted: searching by last name is fast (prefix). Searching by first name only (b,c) does not use the index. Covering = “the phone book already has number + zip, so you don’t need to look up the full address.” The index alone was sufficient.
e3.why: Index interview topics have evolved — not just “add an index” but also thinking about column order and covering. Leftmost prefix is a classic question. Put the column used for both filter and join first.
gotchas: Just remember: composite = leftmost prefix rule; covering = index-only scan.
Interview: place the high-selectivity column first in the index.
IN vs range: WHERE a IN (…) is usable but order matters.

Can only start from the left side of the index — cannot use b or c without a.

All query data comes from the index — fastest read.

sql11.name: Query optimization — EXPLAIN ANALYZE
sql11.desc: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows how the database executes your query with actual timing. Seq Scan on large tables = missing index. Index Scan = using an index (fast). Compare estimated vs actual rows for stale statistics.
sql11.q: How do you read an EXPLAIN ANALYZE output? What should you look for?
sql11.qsub: What does a Seq Scan on a million-row table indicate? How do you fix it?
sql11.what:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE often shows the query's execution plan together with actual timings. If it's slow, you know: Seq Scan (full scan of a million-row table) = missing/ineffective index. Index Scan/Index Only Scan = using an index.

Compare the estimated rows vs actual — large gaps indicate stale statistics or wrong casts. Filter reduction %. Memory for sort/hash = memory consumption. In short: “where are all rows coming from, where are they processed.”
sql11.analogy: Google Maps route: EXPLAIN = the planned route “you will go this way” (full scan vs index). ANALYZE = “what actually happened and it took 12 ms” (real). First look at the route — if you see “drive around the whole city,” change the path (add an index).
sql11.why: Performance is not magic — you must read the plan. Interview: “query is slow, how do you debug?” — EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the first tool. Senior developers don’t just say “add an index,” they look at the plan. This skill places indexes and statistics in the right places.
cons: Runs the query (be careful with writes).
Estimates can be wrong, so don’t be overconfident.
gotchas: Just remember: EXPLAIN ANALYZE = plan + real timing; a large Seq Scan means consider an index.
Interview: EXPLAIN without ANALYZE does not run the query but provides a plan.
ANALYZE on DML runs the full write — be careful in production.
terms: Shows the query plan — what strategy the DB will choose.
Provides the plan plus actual timings.
Reads the entire table — a red flag on large tables.
Selective reads using an index — good.
Estimates vs real — indicates stale statistics.
sql11.visualCap: Seq Scan = full table; Index Scan = selective. Estimated vs actual.

sql14.name: Pivot / Unpivot — row-to-column conversion
sql14.desc: PIVOT rotates rows into columns — like rotating a table 90 degrees. Most databases use CASE WHEN instead of native PIVOT. ROLLUP adds subtotals. CUBE adds subtotals for all combinations.
sql14.q: How do you pivot rows into columns using CASE WHEN?
sql14.qsub: What is the difference between ROLLUP and CUBE? When would you use each?
sql14.what:
PIVOT rotates the table 90° — rows' values become columns. MySQL — T-SQL/Oracle native PIVOT; in databases like PostgreSQL it is built with CASE WHEN + GROUP BY.

ROLLUP — child-total hierarchy: department subtotals + overall total. CUBE — ALL combinations. This is for reporting: "sale by month, by region, by month×region". GROUPING SETS (manual list) provides more control.
sql14.analogy: Table of timings: each row is a class+slot. PIVOT = make each slot a column — Monday row contains "Math, Eng...". ROLLUP = college-wise total + overall rank; CUBE = college, course, slot — we also get combinations. Manual CASE WHEN = "where slot = sun, put it in column sun".
sql14.why: In crosstab/reporting interviews, they ask about the pivot pattern. CASE WHEN is a portable answer (works across DB vendors). Multi-aggregate (subtotals) – extra like ROLLUP. Easy pointer: rotated matrix = PIVOT.
gotchas: Just remember: pivot = rows→columns; CASE WHEN = magic; ROLLUP = subtotal.
Interview: dynamic pivot (many products) = crosstab function / build dynamic SQL.
ROLLUP vs CUBE: rollup = hierarchy, cube = all combos.
terms: Rows rotated into columns — 90 degree rotate.
Manual way to implement PIVOT — condition per column.
sql14.visualCap: PIVOT: rows→columns (CASE WHEN). ROLLUP: subtotal + grand total.

dd2.name: Normalization — 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF
dd2.desc: Normalization eliminates data redundancy. 1NF: atomic values. 2NF: no partial dependencies. 3NF: no transitive dependencies. BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key. Most production DBs normalize to 3NF.
dd2.q: What are 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF? Give an example of violating each.
dd2.qsub: What is a transitive dependency? How does 3NF eliminate it?
dd2.what:
Normalization protects data from redundancy — the same value is not repeated, and updates happen in one place. Grades: 1NF: atomic cells (separate rows for lists). 2NF: remove partial dependency (no column depends on only part of a composite key). 3NF: transitive — city → zip (city inferred from zip) when a non-key depends on another non-key, move to a separate table. BCNF: strict 3NF.

Production mostly normalizes to 3NF. Removing redundancy eliminates update anomalies (forgetting to update multiple places).
dd2.analogy: Student and course list: a cell containing "Math, Eng" — violates 1NF (split into rows). If student_id (1,2) is composite and "student_name" depends only on part of the key — violates 2NF. If course_id → teacher_name → dept (transitive) — violates 3NF. Separate tables; clean.
dd2.why: Interview core: "explain 1NF/2NF/3NF with example". This is the first quality gate in schema design. Know BCNF (remember 2NF/3NF). "Why normalize?" → redundancy + anomalies.
gotchas: Just remember: 1 atomic, 2 no partial, 3 no transitive; BCNF = every determinant is a key.
Interview: 3NF famous "employee, dept_code, dept_name" example.
Normalization = correctness; denormalization = speed — balance.
terms: Atomic values — each column holds a single value; break repeated groups.
No partial dependency — non-key column must depend on the whole key.
No transitive dependency — non-key does not depend on another non-key.
Every determinant must be a key — strict.
Duplicate data — root of update anomalies.
dd2.visualCap: Normalization ladder: 1NF atomic → 2NF no partial → 3NF no transitive.
codeSwap: dept sirf teacher par, teacher→dept = transitive
dept depends only on teacher, teacher→dept = transitive

dd5.name: Denormalization — pre-joined tables, cached aggregates
dd5.desc: Denormalization intentionally adds redundancy for speed. Instead of JOINing 3 tables on every load, copy data into one table. Trade: faster reads but more complex updates and data inconsistency risk.
dd5.q: When should you denormalize a database schema?
dd5.qsub: What are the risks of denormalization? How do materialized views provide controlled denormalization?
dd5.what:
Denormalization deliberately adds redundancy to gain speed. In a 3NF normalized schema each read may require 3-4 JOINs; in a denormalized schema a single table provides fast reads, but writes must pay attention to consistency.

Patterns: pre-joined tables (copy user_name from user table into order table), denormalized aggregates (order count stored on the user row). Controlled approach: materialized views — maintained by DB REFRESH. Trade: reads fast ↔ updates complex, data may become stale.
dd5.analogy: Phone directory + daily call counts: joining the user table for every call is costly → store the user name directly in the order (pre-join). Also keep the count on the user row (cached aggregate). The duplicate means — if the user name changes, existing orders will still show the old name (inconsistency risk), but reporting is fast.
dd5.why: Interview: "when denormalize?" — for read-heavy hot paths. This is a good answer because it avoids slow JOINs. Materialized view keeps denormalization controlled — a production best practice.
gotchas: Just remember: denorm = intentional redundancy for fast reads; sync must be handled.
Interview: name change leaves old logs unchanged — acceptable in some cases.
CQRS/event could keep denorm fresh — advanced answer.
terms: Intentional redundancy — fewer JOINs for faster reads.
Result of a JOIN stored beforehand — no JOIN in the query.
SUM/COUNT pre-computed — not recomputed on every query.
Controlled denormalization — maintained by the DB.
Duplicate copy can become stale — requires synchronization.
dd5.visualCap: Denormalized: user name copied into orders → no JOIN. But sync risk.

dd1.name: ER Diagrams — entities, relationships, cardinality
dd1.desc: ER modeling is a blueprint drawn before SQL. Entities (things), Attributes (properties), Relationships (connections). Cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N) defines how entities relate. M:N becomes a junction table.
dd1.q: How do you model a many-to-many relationship in a relational database?
dd1.qsub: What is the difference between a strong entity and a weak entity?
dd1.what:
ER diagram is a blueprint created before SQL. Entities = things (tables), attributes = columns, relationships + cardinality = the relationship count (1:1, 1:N, M:N).

M:N (students many courses) is not modeled directly in a relational schema — create a junction table (enrollments) with student_id + course_id (each becomes 1:N). A weak entity cannot exist without a parent (order_items without an order).
dd1.analogy: House planning blueprint: first draw rooms (entities) and doors (relations), then build with bricks (SQL). "How many rooms connect to how many rooms"? — 1:1, 1:N, M:N. Students↔Courses M:N is like a stair-case plan — connect them with a "junction corridor" (enrollment).
dd1.why: Interview question "Design a schema for X" always starts with an ER diagram. Understanding cardinality and creating a junction table is a core skill. The difference between strong and weak entities is also asked. Smart approach: start with ER, then write SQL.
gotchas: Just remember: M:N = junction table; cardinality line; weak entity = parent-dependent.
Interview: give the M:N junction a composite primary key.
One-to-one rarely needed — same table/same PK enough.
terms: Thing to model — User, Order, Product (each table).
M:N implemented with two tables plus a link table.
Cannot exist without its parent — e.g., order items.
dd1.visualCap: M:N → junction table. Cardinality 1:N standard. Weak entity = dependent.

f4.name: Schema patterns — STI, CTI; Embedding vs Referencing
f4.desc: Single Table Inheritance puts all types in one table with nullable columns. Class Table Inheritance uses base + type-specific tables. In NoSQL: Embedding stores data inside the document, Referencing stores IDs.
f4.q: When would you use embedding vs referencing in MongoDB?
f4.qsub: What are the trade-offs between Single Table Inheritance and Class Table Inheritance?
f4.what:
STI stores all types in a single table (user + admin in the same table, unused columns are NULL). Simple, fast reads, but null-heavy and a widening schema. CTI – base table holds all common columns; subclasses are in separate tables with foreign keys. Clean, but a JOIN is always required.

In NoSQL: embedding stores related data inside the document (address inside user) – reads with a single query; referencing stores only IDs in a separate collection. Embed for 1:1 or 1:few relationships that are read together; reference for many or independent relationships.
f4.analogy: Office register: STI = a register – each type has its own empty slots (NULL) to fill; CTI = base register (name) plus type-specific diaries (salary, projects) linked. NoSQL: embedding = "address card stapled in the user's file", referencing = "address card in a separate cabinet, with its number in the file".
f4.why: Schema patterns drive every modeling decision in production. STI vs CTI – Rails-style legacy; Embed vs Reference – a favorite MongoDB interview question. “When embed when reference?” – high-signal answer.
gotchas: Just remember: STI/CTI = table inheritance choice; embed vs reference = NoSQL join logic.
Interview: embedding a one-to-many large list hits the document limit (16 MB).
Reference + application-level denormalization = common hybrid.
terms: Single Table Inheritance – a single table, types stored in nullable columns.
Class Table Inheritance – base table + type-specific tables + FK.
NoSQL (Mongo): data stored inside – no JOIN.
IDs stored – multiple documents, joiner needed.
A concept with many shapes – modeling choice.
f4.visualCap: STI: everything in one table + NULLs. Embed: data inside. Reference: only IDs.

dd6.name: Star Schema & Snowflake Schema
dd6.desc: Star schema: central fact table (metrics) surrounded by dimension tables (attributes). Snowflake normalizes dimensions. Star is preferred for query performance. Fact tables are deep and narrow.
dd6.q: What is the difference between a star schema and a snowflake schema?
dd6.qsub: What is a slowly changing dimension? How do Type 1 and Type 2 handle changes over time?
dd6.what:
Star schema is the standard for analytics: a central fact table (measures, millions of numbers) surrounded by denormalized dimension tables (dates, products). Each fact row contains foreign keys to the dimensions. Snowflake normalizes the dimensions to 2NF – less redundancy but more joins.

Star is fast (flat, direct joins) and therefore preferred. Slowly Changing Dimensions: when a dimension changes (e.g., customer location), Type 1 overwrites the existing row (simple, history lost), Type 2 adds a new version row (history preserved).
dd6.analogy: Mathematical map: fact = "how much sold" numbers at the center. Dimensions = "when (date), what (product), where (store)" – their codes form the axes. Star: each axis is a single line, no nested maze. Snowflake: axes are broken into further sub-levels, creating more pieces. SCD example: a customer's city changes – Type 1 overwrites (strong), Type 2 adds a new lineage row.
dd6.why: Analytics/interview: "design a sales warehouse" – star schema evaluation. SCD 2 answer often breaks other embedding questions. "Star vs snowflake" – performance vs flexibility.
gotchas: Just remember: star = fact + flat dimensions; snowflake = normalized dimensions; SCD2 = version rows magic.
Interview: fact narrow + deep; dimension wide + shallow.
Keep the distinction between numeric 0 and NULL for measures.
terms: Center – numeric measures (sales amount), deep, many rows.
Fact + flattened dimensions – single join level, fast.
Dimensions normalized further – less redundancy, more joins.
SCD: dimensions change (address). Type 1 overwrites, Type 2 creates version rows.
dd6.visualCap: Star: fact center + flat dimensions. Snowflake: dimensions normalized.

tx1.name: ACID properties — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability
tx1.desc: ACID guarantees reliable transactions. Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: valid state transitions. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere. Durability: committed data survives crashes.
tx1.q: Explain each ACID property with a real-world example.
tx1.qsub: How is atomicity implemented in PostgreSQL? What role does the write-ahead log play?
tx1.what:
ACID transaction guarantee: Atomicity – either both operations happen (e.g., debit 200 and credit 100) or none. Consistency – after the transaction, all constraints (foreign keys, checks) remain valid. Isolation – even when run concurrently, results appear as if each transaction ran separately. Durability – once committed, the data remains visible after a crash.

In PostgreSQL, atomicity and durability are provided by the WAL: each change is first written to the log, then to the data page. After a crash, WAL is used to redo changes – nothing is lost.
tx1.analogy: Gift transfer (A → B 100): Atomicity = both sides credit-debit perfectly or none. Consistency = the store's rules (balance ≥ 0) are never broken. Isolation = even if two accounts are updated together, they behave as if the updates were sequential. Durability = a receipt is created (WAL) – even if the store loses power you can restore the ₹100 credit.
tx1.why: ACID is the foundation for every transaction and concurrency interview question. "Consistency vs Isolation", "What does WAL do" – core DB internals. It also explains why full-DB transactions are preferred over file-based approaches.
gotchas: Just remember: Atomicity box, Consistency rules, Isolation isolation, Durability = trust in WAL.
Interview: autocommit makes each query its own transaction – use explicit BEGIN/COMMIT for multi-step work.
Durability config: synchronous_commit = off → faster but riskier.
terms: All-or-nothing – no intermediate state inside the transaction.
Valid state according to DB rules – constraints hold.
Concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other.
Data is permanent after commit – even after a crash.
Write-Ahead Log – log first, then data; basis for recovery.
tx1.visualCap: ACID: all-or-nothing, valid rules, no interference, survives crash (WAL).
svgSwap: redo from the log on a crash

tx2.name: Isolation levels — Read Committed to Serializable
tx2.desc: Isolation levels control how much one transaction can see of others work. READ COMMITTED (default), REPEATABLE READ, SERIALIZABLE. Higher isolation reduces anomalies but reduces concurrency.
tx2.q: What is the difference between READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ?
tx2.qsub: What anomalies can occur at each isolation level? How does Snapshot Isolation work?
tx2.what:
Isolation levels determine how much a transaction can see of another's work. Four levels: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads allowed), READ COMMITTED (no dirty reads – PostgreSQL default), REPEATABLE READ (snapshot – same query returns the same answer), SERIALIZABLE (as if all transactions run serially).

Anomalies: dirty read (seeing uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (same query returns different results), phantom (new rows appear). Higher isolation = safer, less concurrency. PostgreSQL’s MVCC makes REPEATABLE READ inexpensive.
tx2.analogy: Exam hall copies: READ COMMITTED = the latest ink on each question (the answer can change on a second read). REPEATABLE READ = a paper copy taken at the gate – the same copy for the entire exam period. SERIALIZABLE = only one person receives the paper at a time; everyone else waits – safest but slowest. Dirty read = reading ink that hasn't dried – unreadable.
tx2.why: Interview: "Which isolation level? Why is Read Committed the default?" – understanding PostgreSQL’s REPEATABLE READ and phantom handling. The isolation-consistency dial is core OLTP knowledge. Most read/write bugs stem from these concepts.
gotchas: Just remember: PG default = Read Committed; Repeatable = snapshot; anomalies: dirty, non-repeatable, phantom.
Interview: PostgreSQL’s REPEATABLE READ also blocks phantoms (ledger-based).
On SERIALIZABLE failure, implement a retry loop.
terms: How much of another transaction is visible – four levels.
PostgreSQL default – only committed data, each statement gets its own snapshot.
Snapshot taken at transaction start – repeated queries return the same result.
As if transactions run serially – highest level, all anomalies blocked.
Dirty read, non-repeatable, phantom – controlled by isolation levels.
tx2.visualCap: Levels: left strict-safe (serial) → right lenient (read uncommitted).
svgSwap: a fresh snapshot for each statement
codeSwap: High level => kam anomalies, kam concurrency.
High level => fewer anomalies, less concurrency.

no5.name: Graph databases — Neo4j, Cypher
no5.desc: Graph databases store nodes (things) and edges (relationships). Perfect when relationships are as important as data — social networks, fraud detection, recommendations. Cypher query language uses ASCII art syntax.
no5.q: When would you choose a graph database over a relational database?
no5.qsub: How does traversal depth affect performance in a graph database?
no5.what:
Graph databases make relationships first-class citizens. Nodes + directed labelled edges. As if relationships are the data — social graph, fraud rings, recommendations. Cypher = ASCII-art SQL: MATCH (a)-[:FRIEND]->(b) — (persons) -relation- (persons).

In relational databases, a 6-JOIN friendship depth is brutal; in a graph, traversal is natural. However, as traversal depth increases, the count explodes — this is the graph's hidden cost.
no5.analogy: Wedding cat: a line of friends' photos + a "this couple is married" tape (edges). "Who is Sam's friend's friend's friend?" — follow the line (traverse). Relational = copying the joining register everywhere (JOINs); graph = just look and move on. But the farther you go (depth), the larger the crowd also grows.
no5.why: Interview: "Why relational vs graph?" — relationship-heavy depth queries. Fraud (2-hop accounts), recommendations, social — graph shows its magic. Reading Cypher is an extra plus.
gotchas: Just remember: graph = nodes + labelled edges; multi-hop traversal is king; depth = cost.
Interview: shortest-path and simple search cases can be covered in relational.
Cypher ASCII syntax: (node)-[:REL]->(node).
terms: Following relationships to discover paths — depth matters.
no5.visualCap: Nodes + labelled edges. Depth traversal = natural. Relational = MANY joins.

g7.name: Time-series databases — InfluxDB, TimescaleDB
g7.desc: Time-series databases optimize for append-heavy, time-ordered data like metrics and sensor readings. TimescaleDB extends PostgreSQL with automatic time-based partitioning. Append-only, never updates past readings.
g7.q: What makes a time-series database different from a regular database?
g7.qsub: What is downsampling and why is it essential for long-term metric retention?
g7.what:
Time-series databases for metrics/sensors: data is append-only, always time-prefixed, past updates are not allowed. TimescaleDB = PostgreSQL + time partitioning (hypertables) — still SQL. InfluxDB — purpose-built, TSM compression + downsampling.

Downsampling: 1-minute raw data becomes 1-hour average after a few months — retention by lines. This makes long-term storage light. Regular DB struggles with time-range joins; TS DB optimizes time-order I/O.
g7.analogy: Weather station diary: record temperature every minute (append). Never modify an old entry (append-only). A year of 1-minute data is heavy — therefore after a month compute hourly averages (downsample), after 10 years delete (retention). In a normal DB diary you have to read the whole page; TS DB gives you the entry column instantly by date.
g7.why: Interview: "Where should monitoring/observability data be stored?" — TSDB. Downsampling + retention = scaling storage conversation. Timescale = PG + time-series ecosystem. Real-world system design (metrics pipeline).
gotchas: Just remember: TS = append-only + time-partition; downsampling + retention = storage control.
Interview: hypertable on PostgreSQL means full SQL remains.
High cardinality (many devices) leads to series explosion.
terms: Time-stamped data — append heavy, never update. InfluxDB, TimescaleDB.
Coarse aggregation of old data — reduces storage.
Automatic deletion policy for old data.
g7.visualCap: Append-only time series. Downsample old → compact. Retention drops ancient.

g8.name: Vector databases — Pinecone, pgvector, HNSW
g8.desc: Vector databases store high-dimensional embeddings for semantic search. AI models convert text into numbers — similar meanings produce close vectors. Powers RAG: retrieve relevant docs via vector search, feed to LLM.
g8.q: How do vector databases enable semantic search?
g8.qsub: What is the difference between HNSW and IVF indexing for approximate nearest neighbor search?
g8.what:
Vector databases store AI embeddings and provide similarity search. The vectors for "Hello" and "Hi" will be close — search "what is near 'hi'". This is not an exact match, but meaning-based.

At scale, exact nearest is impossible — ANN algorithms: HNSW (graph layers, balanced quality/speed) vs IVF (clusters, fast build). RAG — retrieve relevant docs before the LLM. pgvector = vectors in PostgreSQL (SQL remains).
g8.analogy: Word atlas (meaning map): each word has coordinates — "banana" and "apple" are close, "CPU" is far. Search "what is near 'flower'" = direction on the map, any word. In a large map, finding the exact gap is slow — HNSW = "shrink the neighborhood step by step"; IVF = "first cluster by city". RAG = extract relevant snippets from the map and give them to the expert (LLM).
g8.why: AI-era interview topic — semantic search, RAG. HNSW vs IVF — indexed design discussion. pgvector vs Pinecone — self-hosted vs managed. This is common in current hiring rounds.
gotchas: Just remember: vector = meaning coordinates; ANN (HNSW/IVF) = scale search; RAG = retrieve + LLM.
Interview: exact kNN impractical — hence ANN.
Match the embedding model metric (cosine vs dot) to the index.
terms: Store of high-dimensional embeddings + similarity search. Pinecone, pgvector.
Text/image → number vector — meaning as distance.
Retrieve relevant docs → feed LLM — role of vector DB.
g8.visualCap: Embeddings: meaning → vector space. ANN (HNSW/IVF) finds close neighbors fast.

ddb2.name: Sharding — hash, range, consistent hashing
ddb2.desc: Sharding splits data across multiple servers. Hash sharding distributes evenly. Range sharding enables range queries but risks hot spots. Cross-shard JOINs are expensive or impossible.
ddb2.q: What is the difference between hash sharding and range sharding?
ddb2.qsub: What is consistent hashing? How does it minimize data movement when nodes join or leave?
ddb2.what:
Sharding divides a table's data across multiple nodes when a single node cannot handle the load. Hash sharding: assign node based on key hash — even distribution, but range queries need all nodes. Range sharding: date/user-id bins — range query fast, but a "hot" bin consumes all traffic.

Consistent hashing: place nodes on a circle; when a node leaves, only a small segment is reassigned — not the whole ring. Re-sharding/scaling = headache; therefore use buckets + virtual nodes.
ddb2.analogy: Large library with many shelves: hash = compute a hash of the book title to decide shelf "3" — even filling, but to find "authors A-K" (range) you need all shelves. Range = you pick the A-K shelf — easy to find an author but the "Z" shelf may become hot with many books. Consistent ring = when adding a shelf, only 1-2 neighboring shelves are affected, the rest stay in place.
ddb2.why: System-design interview "scale the DB" — sharding is the first answer. Discuss hash vs range, hot spots, rebalancing cost. Also mention cross-shard JOIN/ACID limits for senior-level depth.
gotchas: Just remember: hash = even distribution, range = ordered + hot; consistent hash = minimal rebalance.
Interview: sharding + global index queries = fan-out.
Join queries across shards must be designed to be avoided.
terms: Distribute data across multiple servers — horizontal scaling.
key_hash % N — even spread, range queries suffer.
Based on key range — range scans work, hot spots possible.
When a node is added/removed, only a few keys move.
ddb2.visualCap: Hash = even spread (range suffers). Range = ordered (hot spots). Consistent = minimal moves.

tx4.name: MVCC — Multi-Version Concurrency Control
