tx4.desc: MVCC keeps multiple versions of each row so readers and writers never block each other. Readers see old versions, writers create new ones. Postgres uses xmin/xmax columns. VACUUM cleans old versions.
tx4.q: How does MVCC allow readers and writers to work simultaneously?
tx4.qsub: What are xmin and xmax in PostgreSQL? What happens if vacuum does not run?
tx4.what:
MVCC PostgreSQL's secret: each row has multiple versions. The writer creates a new version, readers see the old version according to their snapshot — therefore reader and writer do not block.

PG rows have xmin (which transaction created it) and xmax (which transaction deleted/updated it) — snapshot rules use these to decide which version to show. Old versions remain until VACUUM cleans them — if vacuum does not run, bloat occurs (storage grows and the table slows).
tx4.analogy: Homework notebook carbon copies: each update creates a new blank copy (new version). The teacher (reader) holds the copy from the start of the class — can read until a new class copy appears. The copy board (xmin/xmax) indicates which version was taken by whom. Each day when the sun rises, burn the old copy (VACUUM) — otherwise the room fills up.
tx4.why: Interview concurrency core: "how do PostgreSQL reads/writes avoid blocking?" → MVCC. xmin/xmax, snapshot isolation, vacuum. This also shows PostgreSQL's fundamental improvement over row-lock databases.
cons: Bloat if vacuum does not run.
gotchas: Just remember: MVCC = versions + snapshot; reader/writer do not block; vacuum cleanup.
Interview: a long-running transaction keeps a log slice — vacuum cannot remove the corresponding rows.
Auto-vacuum is always on; tune it via table design.
terms: Multi-Version Concurrency Control — each row has many versions.
The transaction that created the row — visibility.
The transaction that deleted/updated the row — version store.
Cleanup of old versions — bloat control.
where: "how do reads and writes avoid blocking?"
tx4.visualCap: MVCC: writer = new version, reader = old snapshot; VACUUM clears old.
svgSwap: the reader gets its own point-in-time

tx5.name: Locking — row-level, intent locks, deadlocks
tx5.desc: Shared locks allow multiple readers but block writers. Exclusive locks block everyone. Deadlock occurs when transactions wait for each other in a cycle. Database detects and kills one transaction.
tx5.q: What is the difference between shared and exclusive locks? When is each used?
tx5.qsub: How does a database detect deadlocks? What is the wait-for graph?
tx5.what:
Locks manage concurrency: shared (READ — many can hold it simultaneously, no writer), exclusive (WRITE — one holder, others wait). Intent locks are table-level signals that row locks will follow.

Deadlock occurs when A holds row1, B holds row2; A requests row2, B requests row1 — both wait. The DB builds a wait-for graph, detects the cycle, and rolls back one victim (choosing a victim to break the cycle).
tx5.analogy: A single-page notebook: shared = many can read (but no changes). Exclusive = someone is writing — others must take another line. Deadlock = student A wants B's page, B wants A's page — both stuck. The teacher (DB) sees the cycle and says "A, give up" (rollback) — that student's paper is discarded.
tx5.why: Interview concurrency focus: row vs table locks, deadlock cycles and detection, victim rollback. "Why deadlocks occur and how to avoid them" — lock ordering best practice.
gotchas: Just remember: shared = readers, exclusive = writer; deadlock = cycle → DB rolls back a victim.
Interview: lock deferral — the smaller the lock window, the fewer deadlocks.
Use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE only when necessary.
terms: Read lock — multiple readers allowed, writer blocked.
Write lock — only one holder, all others blocked.
Transaction A waits for B, B waits for A — a cycle.
Deadlock detection: who is waiting for whom.
Table-level hint that row locks will be acquired.
tx5.visualCap: Shared = readers; Exclusive = one writer. Deadlock cycle → DB rolls back victim.
codeSwap: Deadlock avoid: hamesha same order (id ascending) se lock.
Deadlock avoidance: always lock in the same order (id ascending).

ddb4.name: Distributed transactions — 2PC, 3PC, Saga pattern
ddb4.desc: Two-Phase Commit coordinates distributed transactions: prepare phase then commit phase. Problem: coordinator crash blocks everyone. Saga pattern fixes this with local transactions and compensating actions.
ddb4.q: What is the problem with Two-Phase Commit? How does the Saga pattern address it?
ddb4.qsub: What is the difference between choreography-based and orchestration-based sagas?
ddb4.what:
Distributed transactions span multiple services/nodes — need a global commit. 2PC: phase 1 prepare (all say "ready"), phase 2 commit — if any fail, all abort. Problem: if the coordinator crashes, everything blocks. 3PC adds a pre-commit phase for better crash recovery, but it is still not perfect under network partitions.

Saga pattern is a modern solution: no global transaction — a sequence of local transactions plus compensating actions (logical rollback). Choreography uses events for flow; orchestration uses a controller.
ddb4.analogy: Group picnic plan: 2PC = each person says "I can go" on a call (prepare), then everyone confirms (commit). If anyone cannot go — everyone cancels (rollback). If the coordinator forgets — the picnic never starts. Saga = plan proceeds step-by-step; if a step fails, subsequent steps are "canceled back" to compensate — no global rule.
ddb4.why: Microservices interviews often focus on this topic. 2PC's blocking flaw versus saga's compensating fix — a clear contrast. "When to use 2PC vs saga" — financial consistency versus availability.
gotchas: Just remember: 2PC = coordinator blocks; saga = local + compensate; orchestrated vs choreographed.
Interview: make compensating actions idempotent.
In saga, use an outbox/queue to guarantee delivery.
terms: Prepare + pre-commit + commit — better coordinator crash recovery.
Local transactions + compensating actions — no global lock.
Saga driven by events — messages, no central coordinator.
Saga driven by a central orchestrator.
ddb4.visualCap: 2PC: coordinator prepares all then commits. Saga: local steps + compensate.

no1.name: CAP Theorem — Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance
no1.desc: CAP theorem: a distributed system can only guarantee 2 of 3 properties. Since partitions are unavoidable, you choose CP (consistent, may refuse requests) or AP (available, may return stale data).
no1.q: Explain the CAP theorem. What is the difference between CP and AP systems?
no1.qsub: What is PACELC? How does it extend CAP with latency/consistency trade-offs in normal operation?
no1.what:
CAP theorem: a distributed system can guarantee only two of the three properties when a network partition occurs — Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance. Partition is unavoidable (networks fail), so you choose: CP (e.g., Mongo) — consistent but with downtime/reduced availability, or AP (e.g., Cassandra, DynamoDB) — available but may return stale data.

During normal operation all three can be satisfied — CAP's tension appears only during a partition. PACELC extends this: even without a partition there is a latency vs consistency trade-off.
no1.analogy: Two shops, a highway blocked: partition = road closed. CP = "don't sell without the latest price" (safe, shop closed) — consistent but unavailable. AP = "sell whatever price is known" (shop open, price may be stale). When the highway reopens, prices are reconciled.
no1.why: NoSQL interview introductions often start with "why the consistency trade-offs?" This is fundamental; every distributed store mentions it. Rank CAP examples in your answers — it's a key signal.
gotchas: Just remember: when a partition occurs you must choose either CP or AP; partitions are unavoidable; CP is safer, AP is more available.
Interview: "pick 2 of 3" — incorrect framing; partitions always happen.
The same database can offer both modes (e.g., Mongo strong vs majority).
terms: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance — any two of the three.
Every read sees the latest write.
Every request receives a response as long as a node is up.
CP = provides consistency (requests may be rejected); AP = provides availability (stale data may be returned).
no1.visualCap: CAP: when a partition occurs choose CP (consistent, no answer) vs AP (answers, maybe stale).
codeSwap: conflict without a lock — client/actor decides.

no6.name: BASE vs ACID — consistency trade-offs
no6.desc: BASE is the NoSQL consistency model: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually Consistent. The opposite of ACID. System always responds, data may be temporarily inconsistent, eventually all replicas converge.
no6.q: What is BASE? How does it differ from ACID?
no6.qsub: When is eventual consistency acceptable? Give examples where it is not.
no6.what:
BASE is the NoSQL counterpart to ACID — not ACID but focuses on availability and scale. Basically Available: every request receives an answer. Soft state: data in replicas can be continuously updated. Eventually consistent: data may be slightly stale for a while, but eventually all replicas become the same.

Use when: leaderboards, likes, cache, follower feeds — where slightly stale data is acceptable. NOT: money, inventory — where ACID is required.
no6.analogy: Sharing a WhatsApp status: you write it, it appears instantly on your phone. It shows up on friends' phones after a short delay (eventually). No guaranteed exact state (soft state) — the system just remains. The opposite, a currency transfer, is ACID — immediate, exact, correct.
no6.why: Interview "BASE vs ACID" — NoSQL consistency terminology. The “when is eventual OK” answer demonstrates approval-savvy knowledge. It also makes the AP side of CAP concrete.
gotchas: Just remember: BASE = available + eventually consistent; ACID = strict + exact.
Interview: "when NOT BASE" — money, race conditions.
Eventual = "at some future point", not "immediate".
terms: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually Consistent — NoSQL.
Copy's data can change over time (no fixed state).
After some time all copies become equal.
no6.visualCap: BASE: always available, eventually consistent. ACID: exact + strict.

no2.name: Key-Value stores — Redis, DynamoDB
no2.desc: Key-value stores are the simplest NoSQL model: key maps to value. Redis stores everything in RAM for sub-millisecond speed. Supports data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets. TTL for auto-expiry.
no2.q: What are the use cases for Redis? When would you choose it over a relational database?
no2.qsub: What is the difference between Redis persistence options RDB and AOF?
no2.what:
Key-Value store is the simplest model — a key maps to a value, O(1) get/set. Redis keeps everything in RAM — sub-millisecond latency, data structures (string, hash, list, set, sorted set), TTL expiry, and persistence options RDB (point-in-time snapshot) vs AOF (append-only log, granular). DynamoDB is AWS-managed, partitioned and replicated, with auto-scaling.

Consistency configuration: Redis is single-threaded with strong consistency; DynamoDB defaults to eventual consistency (strong optional). Use cases are typically caching, sessions, or rate-limiting.
no2.analogy: A small pocket diary: number → name instantly (O(1)). Redis is a diary in RAM — when the diary is closed you still need a copy: RDB = photocopy (full snapshot), AOF = note-by-note add-on log (records every change). TTL = “forget this page by tomorrow morning” (automatic expiry).
no2.why: Caching interview questions often highlight Redis as unbeatable. TTL, evictions, RDB vs AOF are real production decisions. KV lookups are also the preferred store in microservices.
gotchas: Just remember: KV = O(1); Redis = RAM + TTL + structures; RDB snapshot vs AOF log.
Interview: Redis single-threaded — avoid blocking commands (KEYS).
AOF vs RDB: AOF granular, RDB point-in-time fast.
terms: The simplest: key → value lookup. Redis, DynamoDB.
In RAM — sub-ms; strings, lists, sets, sorted sets.
AWS managed — KV + documents, replica scaling.
Redis: RDB snapshot + AOF append log.
no2.visualCap: Redis: RAM + data structures + TTL. Persistence: RDB snapshot vs AOF log.

no3.name: Document stores — MongoDB, Firestore
no3.desc: Document stores save JSON-like documents where each can have different structure. Great for flexible schemas. MongoDB organizes documents into collections. Embedding related data inside documents avoids JOINs.
no3.q: When would you choose MongoDB over PostgreSQL?
no3.qsub: What is the 16MB document limit in MongoDB? How does it affect schema design?
no3.what:
Document stores save JSON-like documents — each document has a flexible structure. MongoDB uses collections (tables), and embedding (related data inside) eliminates the need for JOINs. Firestore is similar — popular for realtime sync.

Trade-off: flexible schema enables quick development but makes predicting read patterns harder. MongoDB limits documents to 16 MB — therefore embedding large lists should be kept small. Relationships are handled either as embeds (1-few) or references (many/independent).
no3.analogy: A personal file for each user: each user has a file, all user-internal data (address, phone) can be embedded — no need to look elsewhere, no merge (JOIN). If orders become a large list, the file may exceed the size limit (16 MB) — those items should be stored in a separate register (referencing). The file stays separate from the grid — otherwise the grid would contain redundant data.
no3.why: Interview: “Why Mongo vs PostgreSQL?” — flexible schema and scale with no JOIN cost versus consistency and joins. Embed vs reference reflects schema philosophy. Document stores are used for product search, profiles, catalogs.
gotchas: Just remember: doc = flexible JSON; embed for 1-few, reference for many; check 16 MB.
Interview: replication default — secondary reads eventual.
Indexes in Mongo: compound and index chaining.
terms: JSON-like docs — each doc can have a different structure. MongoDB, Firestore.
Related data inside the doc — no JOIN.
Reference another doc’s id — requires a lookup.
MongoDB’s maximum size for a single document.
no3.visualCap: Document: flexible JSON. Embed (in doc) vs Reference (ID link).

no4.name: Column-Family stores — Cassandra, HBase
no4.desc: Column-family stores distribute data across nodes using consistent hashing. No single point of failure. Design tables around queries, not data models. No JOINs — create separate tables for each access pattern.
no4.q: Why does Cassandra require query-first data modeling?
no4.qsub: What is the difference between a partition key and a clustering key in Cassandra?
no4.what:
Column-family stores (Cassandra, HBase) keep data as row key + sorted columns and distribute it across nodes using consistent hashing — no single point of failure.

Rule: design tables around queries, not around data. No JOINs — each access pattern gets its own denormalized table. The partition key determines the node; the clustering key defines the order within a partition. Queries must filter by the partition key, otherwise a full cluster scan occurs.
no4.analogy: Safe deposit boxes in a vault: each account has a fixed box assigned by consistent hashing (partition key). Inside the box, items are sorted by time (clustering key). If you search for "this item in this box" — it’s immediate. But searching "this item across all boxes" (no partition key) requires scanning the entire vault — heavy. Design tables after thinking about the queries.
no4.why: Cassandra architecture interview topics — no single point of failure, query-first data model, partition and clustering keys. It is the king of distributed write scale. “Design a write-heavy system” often leads to Cassandra.
gotchas: Just remember: partition key → node; clustering key → order; query-first, no joins.
Interview: WHERE without partition key = full scan.
Consistency ONE vs QUORUM is set per query.
terms: Row key + sorted columns groups — Cassandra, HBase.
Which node the data will go to (consistent hash).
Design queries first, then tables — No JOINs.
When nodes are added/removed, only a small amount of data moves — Cassandra.
no4.visualCap: Partition key → node via consistent hashing. Clustering key = order in partition.
svgSwap: adding joey = a little data moves
codeSwap: JOIN nahi: denormalized table per access path.
No JOINs: a denormalized table per access path.

ddb1.name: Replication — single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless
ddb1.desc: Replication copies data across nodes for fault tolerance and read scaling. Single-leader: one writes, followers copy. Multi-leader: multiple accept writes. Leaderless: any node accepts writes with quorum.
ddb1.q: What is the difference between single-leader and multi-leader replication?
ddb1.qsub: How does leaderless replication handle conflict resolution? What are CRDTs?
ddb1.what:
Replication data copies on nodes — fault tolerance + read scale. Single-leader: one leader writes, followers replay (async/sync). Reads from followers (but lag → stale). Multi-leader: multiple writers — conflict resolution required (LWW, CRDT). Leaderless: any node writes, quorum (W+R > N) ensures reads are fresh — DynamoDB style.

Replication lag affects read-your-write and monotonic reads. Async = fast but data-loss risk on leader crash.
ddb1.analogy: Home notepad + copies: father writes (leader), juniors make copies (replicas). Reading copies is faster but a small delay (lag). Multi-leader = both parents write — duplicate pictures appear in both places — which to prefer? (conflict: last write wins or merge both — CRDT). Leaderless = everyone writes; quorum: 3 will read, 2 must have written = latest will be obtained.
ddb1.why: Interview: replication (leader modes) + lag issues + conflict handling — core of distributed DB discussions. "Why replica lag matters" at product level. Quorum math = engineer reasoning.
gotchas: Remember: single-leader = 1 writer; multi/leaderless = conflict management; quorum W+R>N.
Interview: sync replication = write latency, async = less durable.
LWW (last-write-wins) can drop updates — CRDT better for counters.
terms: One writer (leader), replicas copy — reads scale.
Follower is slightly behind — read-your-write concern.
Do writes same key — LWW, CRDT, vector clocks.
ddb1.visualCap: Single-leader: one writer, followers. Multi-leader/leaderless = write everywhere.
codeSwap: (kisi order ka write read ke overlap)
(a write of some order overlapping a read)

ddb3.name: Consensus — Raft, Paxos
ddb3.desc: Consensus algorithms ensure multiple nodes agree on a value despite failures. Raft: elect leader, leader handles writes, majority must acknowledge. If leader crashes, followers elect a new one.
ddb3.q: How does Raft leader election work? What happens when the leader crashes?
ddb3.qsub: What is the difference between Raft and Paxos? Why is Raft preferred for implementability?
ddb3.what:
Consensus algorithms (Raft, Paxos) keep multiple nodes on a single state despite failures. Raft: leader elected (terms, votes, majority), leader writes to the log, majority ack commits. Leader crash → timeout → new election.

Majority rule prevents split-brain: only one leader at a time. Paxos: correct but hard to learn/implement; therefore Raft is the practical favorite. Use: etcd, ZooKeeper, CockroachDB replication, Kafka controller.
ddb3.analogy: Village council voting: chief election (term → votes → majority). The chief writes orders on all parchments (log). When majority "captures" (commit) — immediate. Chief leaves — new election (new term). Two chiefs? No — in 5 members, 3 votes majority gives one mandate. Raft = simple process; Paxos = mathematically sound but hard to implement (rare).
ddb3.why: Interview: "how do distributed nodes agree?" — leader election, majority, split-brain. Raft easy narrative — terms/timeouts/logs. This is the basis of distributed consistency (ZAB, etcd).
gotchas: Remember: raft = elect + majority log; crash → re-elect; majority prevents split brain.
Interview: quorum N/2+1 — odd cluster sizes.
Disk fsync latency = commit latency.
terms: Nodes agree on a single value — even with failures.
Older consensus — correct but hard to implement.
ddb3.visualCap: Raft: elect leader → majority commits log → crash = re-elect. No split brain.

j5.name: Gossip protocol — peer-to-peer state dissemination
j5.desc: Gossip spreads information without a central coordinator. Each node periodically picks a random neighbor and shares state. After O(log N) rounds, all nodes know. Used by Cassandra for cluster membership.
j5.q: How does the gossip protocol spread information across a cluster?
j5.qsub: What is the Phi Accrual failure detector? How does Cassandra use it?
j5.what:
Gossip protocol — rumor spreading: each node repeatedly sends state to a random neighbor. No single source needed — O(log N) rounds inform everyone. Cassandra/DynamoDB cluster membership is derived here (who is live), without a central list.

Scalable + self-healing (no single point). Phi Accrual failure detector uses heartbeat time gaps to compute the probability that a node has failed — better than a fixed timeout.
j5.analogy: Village gossip: a news item is not told directly to everyone — each person tells 2-3 neighbors. With each round more people learn. In about 10 rounds the whole village knows. If a house does not reply, neighbors suspect "the node might be down" based on timing gaps (phi). No central authority — everyone shares.
j5.why: Interview: "distributed membership without coordinator?" — gossip. Cassandra failure detector — production gossip. Shows cluster self-management internals. "How does a node know the cluster is changing?" — rounds.
gotchas: Remember: gossip = random-pair spreads news; O(log N) rounds; phi = heartbeat suspicion.
Interview: no guarantee of immediate consistency.
Gossip traffic rate needs tuning.
terms: Node tells state to a random peer — O(log N) rounds for everyone.
No central coordinator — each node equal.
Failure detector — heartbeat gap determines suspicion level.
Which nodes are live — maintained via gossip.
All nodes share a single view — after rounds.
j5.visualCap: Gossip: random neighbor → state. O(log N) rounds = everyone knows.

j6.name: CQRS — separate read/write models
j6.desc: CQRS separates write model (normalized, transactional) from read model (pre-computed, optimized). Scale reads and writes independently. Write to Postgres, read from Redis or Elasticsearch.
j6.q: What problem does CQRS solve? When should you NOT use it?
j6.qsub: How do you keep the read model in sync with the write model? What consistency guarantees does it provide?
j6.what:
CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) uses separate models for write and read. Write: normalized/transaction-safe (Postgres). Read: optimized shapes (Redis/Elasticsearch precomputed). Scale both independently — reads may be higher, writes different.

Sync the read model via events (e.g., CDC, outbox) — the whole application becomes eventually consistent. Necessary? No — for simple CRUD it adds overhead. Use when reads/writes are asymmetric and hot queries need denormalization.
j6.analogy: Book: hardcover for the writer and paperback versions for readers. The writer records everything in the register. Readers receive reader-format cards — each view (dashboard A) has its own projection. No reporter needed, loudly. Modern apps — update cards via events. Simple app: keeping the same book for writer and reader is overkill.
j6.why: Interview: "scale reads vs writes differently" — CQRS answer. Ledger → reporting is a real use. Shows event-driven architecture + eventual consistency. Also "when NOT to use CQRS" — judgment.
gotchas: Remember: CQRS = separate write/read models + event sync; only when needed.
Interview: without CQRS simple CRUD has low overhead.
Design for projection rebuild (replay).
terms: Simple CRUD apps — complexity not justified.
j6.visualCap: CQRS: write model + separate read models. Sync via events, eventually.

j7.name: Event Sourcing — append-only event log
j7.desc: Event Sourcing stores every state change as an immutable event instead of current state. Current state is derived by replaying events. Gives complete audit trail and time travel debugging.
j7.q: What is the difference between Event Sourcing and traditional CRUD storage?
j7.qsub: What are projections in event sourcing? How do snapshots improve replay performance?
j7.what:
Event sourcing does not store the current state, but stores every state change as an event (append-only). A balance of 500 means "OPENED(100), DEPOSIT(200), WITHDRAW(?)" — the full history. The current state is derived by replay (projection).

Benefit: full audit trail + time travel. When encryption was added later — the state changed. Drawback: events never update, schema evolution is tricky, replay is slow → snapshots as periodic milestones. Traditional CRUD overwrites; ES only appends.
j7.analogy: Bank passbook (modern app): the balance is not a single number, but every transaction is recorded (DEPOSIT +200, WITHDRAW -50). Each page is an event — never erased. "What is the balance?" = sum of all entries (projection). When there are many pages → a summary (snapshot) every 50 pages — use that for future counts. If the app needs a review — the entire history is available.
j7.why: Event-driven architecture + audit + rebuildable state — a strong interview topic: ES vs CRUD, projections, snapshots. Often paired with CQRS. "Time travel debugging" signals senior-level expertise.
gotchas: Just remember: ES = events append-only; state = projection; snapshot = replay shortcut.
Interview: events never change — use compensating events for bugs.
Snapshot frequency balances stream length and time trade-off.
terms: State is not stored; events are stored — each change is an append-only log.
Deriving current state from events — read model.
j7.visualCap: ES: state = derived by replaying events. Snapshot speeds long replays.

j8.name: CDC — Change Data Capture, Debezium
j8.desc: CDC streams every database change to other systems in real-time by reading the transaction log. No application code changes needed. Debezium reads PostgreSQL WAL and sends events to Kafka.
j8.q: How does log-based CDC work? Why is it better than trigger-based CDC?
j8.qsub: What is the dual-write problem and how does CDC solve it?
j8.what:
CDC turns database changes into a real-time stream by reading the bin/WAL log (insert/update/delete). No application code changes required. Debezium reads the WAL of PostgreSQL/MySQL and sends events to Kafka.

Problem solved: the dual-write gap (app → DB and app → Kafka) where "DB succeeded but Kafka failed". CDC works from the log — no gap, reliable. Uses: sync Elasticsearch, denormalized read models, data-warehouse streaming, event-driven architectures.
j8.analogy: Vibrant diary + reader: the application writes to a register (DB) — like a diary, and the "diary reader" (Debezium) streams each new line to another place (Kafka marketplace) live — without the app knowing. If the app tried to write to the register and also make a separate copy, a failure in the copy would create a dual-write gap (record written but copy missing). A log reader always copies from the source, so there is no gap.
j8.why: Modern data architecture: Postgres → Kafka → search/cache/lake. Interview question: "How do you keep search in sync?" — CDC. Provides a clean answer to the dual-write problem plus the outbox pattern. It bridges event-driven and data-warehouse patterns.
gotchas: Just remember: CDC = WAL stream; Debezium → Kafka; outbox = reliable dual-write fix.
Interview: dual-write = DB succeeds, Kafka fails gap.
Check WAL retention of old records — ensure it meets disaster-recovery requirements.
terms: Change Data Capture — streams database changes in real time.
Transaction log — where inserts/updates/deletes are recorded.
Tool: reads PostgreSQL WAL and sends events to Kafka.
Application writes to DB and Kafka separately — leads to inconsistency.
Event table inside the DB — provides a reliable source.
j8.visualCap: CDC reads WAL → Kafka → sinks. No app code, no dual-write gap.

arch1.name: OLTP vs OLAP — row vs columnar storage
arch1.desc: OLTP handles day-to-day operations with fast single-row queries. OLAP handles analytics scanning millions of rows. OLTP uses row storage. OLAP uses column storage for faster scanning and compression.
arch1.q: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP workloads?
arch1.qsub: Why is columnar storage 10-100x faster for analytics than row storage?
arch1.what:
OLTP handles the app’s daily routine — small queries, simple writes (orders, cart), always row-keyed. OLAP handles analytics — long queries, scanning whole columns, aggregates (reporting), and is fast with a columnar store because only the needed columns are read.

Why separate: OLTP needs fast writes/rows; OLAP needs wide scans. One cannot run on the other’s workload — therefore separate stores (warehouse) or HTAP. Trick: no single DB excels at both — typecasting is required.
arch1.analogy: Grocery store vs MBA report: OLTP = a grocery shop issuing a bill for each item (immediate, per customer). OLAP = quarter-end: "average order of all customers" (open all files, calculate). Computing the average in the grocery store would make customers wait — hence a separate "report room" (warehouse). Columnar = pre-select only the money column, ignore the rest.
arch1.why: Interview: "OLTP vs OLAP" — the first question about database selection. Explaining row vs columnar stores shows senior knowledge. Connects to warehousing and analytics schema design.
gotchas: Just remember: OLTP = row operations + fast writes; OLAP = column scans + aggregations.
Interview: mixing both requires separate stores/ETL.
Columnar updates are expensive — not suitable for OLTP.
terms: Online Transaction Processing — daily app writes/reads, row-based. Postgres/MySQL.
Online Analytical Processing — large scans, aggregations, columnar. Data warehouse.
Data stored row-wise on disk — fits OLTP workloads.
Data stored column-wise — OLAP scans only relevant columns.
Hybrid — both in one system (SingleStore) or hybrid architecture.
arch1.visualCap: OLTP = row-by-row quick ops. OLAP = wide scans on columns.

k2.name: Data warehousing — Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift
k2.desc: Data warehouses consolidate data from multiple sources for analytics. Columnar storage compresses and scans only needed columns. Snowflake separates compute from storage. BigQuery is serverless.
k2.q: What is the difference between ELT and ETL? Why is ELT preferred for modern warehouses?
k2.qsub: How does Snowflake separate compute from storage? What are the cost implications?
k2.what:
Data warehouse is the organization’s analytics hub — data from OLTP sources (orders, users) is ETL-ed into a clean star schema. ELT (modern): load raw data first, then apply SQL transformations (dbt) — flexible and scalable.

Reporting/BI queries are heavy on OLTP; the warehouse uses a separate columnar engine and a schema tuned for analysis. Star schema = fact + dimensions. OLAP cubes/aggregation tables make drill-down fast.
k2.analogy: Separate newspaper office: branches sell independently (OLTP), the office (warehouse) opens in the evening and gathers data from all branches (ETL): cleans and tabulates it. Some loads are delivered today and cleaned later (ELT) — dbt engineers perform the transformation. The reports clerk counts from this office — cross-branch totals.
k2.why: Analytics architecture interview — warehouse vs OLTP, ETL vs ELT, star schema. "How does analytics scale?" — the warehouse answer. It is the center of reporting pipelines and BI tools.
gotchas: Just remember: warehouse = single source for analytics; star = fact+dims; ETL vs ELT choice.
Interview: incremental vs full load — warehouse pipeline design.
CDC flows can make the warehouse real-time.
terms: Central analytics DB — integrated data from multiple sources.
Load first, transform in the DB — modern (dbt).
k2.visualCap: Sources → ETL → Warehouse (star schema) → BI reports.

k3.name: Data Lake & Lakehouse — Delta Lake, Iceberg
k3.desc: Data lakes store raw files cheaply on object storage. Lakehouse adds ACID transactions on top. Delta Lake: Parquet + transaction log. Iceberg: partition evolution. Hudi: incremental processing.
k3.q: What problems does a Data Lakehouse solve that a raw data lake cannot?
k3.qsub: What is time travel in Delta Lake? How does the transaction log work?
k3.what:
Data lake is a torrent of raw files — unstructured on S3, schema on read (define only what you need). Cheap + vast. Lakehouse adds warehouse-like guarantees to lake storage: ACID tables (Delta, Iceberg) enforce schema + time travel. Medallion bronze → silver → gold — the journey from raw to quality.

Warehouse vs lake: warehouse = curated queries; lake = raw exploration + ML. Lakehouse = both. This is the default modern data platform.
k3.analogy: Big house warehouse vs library: data lake = warehouse — all items raw (S3), pull out what you need (schema on read). But the warehouse has no accounting (ACID) — items can be lost. Lakehouse = warehouse + librarian register — each box cataloged (Delta table), transaction-safe, old records also available. Gold shelf = curated books.
k3.why: Modern data platform interview — lake vs warehouse vs lakehouse. Medallion quality layers + Delta/Iceberg = baseline. Senior understanding of "how the data team organizes raw data".
gotchas: Just remember: lake = raw + schema-on-read; lakehouse = ACID lake tables; medallion = quality tiers.
Interview: lake without table format = query planning hard.
Iceberg/Delta = open formats; vendor lock reduced.
terms: Vast store of raw files (S3/GCS) — schema on read.
Write is separate; lake defines schema on read.
Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Hudi — ACID data.
k3.visualCap: Lake = raw on S3. Lakehouse = ACID tables on lake. Medallion = Bronze→Gold.

k4.name: NewSQL — CockroachDB, TiDB, Spanner
k4.desc: NewSQL gives you SQL + ACID + horizontal scaling. CockroachDB: distributed SQL with Raft consensus. Spanner: globally distributed with TrueTime for external consistency. SQL interface, NoSQL scale.
k4.q: How does CockroachDB achieve distributed ACID transactions?
k4.qsub: What is TrueTime in Google Spanner? Why does it require atomic clocks and GPS?
k4.what:
NewSQL = SQL + ACID that horizontally scales — without the sacrifices of NoSQL (Mongo gave up ACID/joins; NewSQL does not). CockroachDB (PostgreSQL compatible, Raft), TiDB (MySQL compatible), Spanner (Google — globally distributed transactions with atomic clocks).

Trade-off: distributed transaction logic is complex; cross-region latency. Use when a single PostgreSQL cannot be scaled up. NewSQL is the modern relational dream: SQL, joins, ACID, internal sharding.
k4.analogy: Single billing for a large mall: a normal DB is a single shop’s register (exact, but in one place). NewSQL is the mall’s central booking system that runs ACID across 50 counters — any counter’s ticket transaction is atomic. Cockroach = register’s computer system like PostgreSQL but with counters + replicas, managed by Raft. Spanner = Google’s super system — counters linked, global atomic clock.
k4.why: Interview: "SQL at scale?" — NewSQL answer. Spanner’s TrueTime novelty + Raft internals. This is the architect-level point about distributed-SQL middle ground.
gotchas: Just remember: NewSQL = SQL+ACID+scale; Raft/TrueTime internals; internal sharding.
Interview: Cockroach = PostgreSQL protocol (no driver changes needed).
NewSQL vs vitess-style sharding: vendor-managed vs app-managed.
terms: SQL + ACID + distributed scale — relational is modern.
PG wire — Raft consensus, kv internals.
Google — global txns + TrueTime (2PC across DC).
Consensus — leader logs replicas, majority commit.
k4.visualCap: NewSQL = full SQL + ACID, distributed. Raft replicates; TrueTime spans DCs.

k5.name: In-memory databases — Redis, Memcached
k5.desc: In-memory databases store data in RAM for microsecond latency. Redis supports rich data structures with AOF/RDB persistence. Memcached is simpler, multi-threaded, no persistence. 100-1000x faster than disk.
k5.q: When would you choose Redis over Memcached?
k5.qsub: What is the Redis eviction policy allkeys-lru? When would you use volatile-lru instead?
k5.what:
In-memory databases keep data in RAM — zero disk I/O, sub-millisecond. Redis is the most known: structures + TTL + optional persistence RDB (snapshot) / AOF (append-only log) — if RAM is lost in a crash, persistence restores it.

RAM limited + expensive → eviction policies (LRU: remove least recently used) + TTL. Disk-DB vs in-memory: disk = durable heavy; in-memory = speed + cache pattern. Hybrid: hot data in-memory layer, source of truth disk DB.
k5.analogy: Chef’s counter: a small counter where everything is served instantly (no moving to the fridge). But when the counter fills up — remove older items (LRU). If the kitchen closes at night (crash) — items are lost — so refill from the morning recipe list (RDB/AOF). The root fridge (disk DB) is slow but reliable — the big feast comes from there.
k5.why: Caching archetype — Redis or Memcached appears in every system design. Persistence RDB vs AOF, TTL, eviction — production know-how + interview. "Why RAM ping is fast" — cache reads peak because of this.
gotchas: Just remember: in-memory = RAM speed + volatile; RDB/AOF persistence; LRU + TTL remember.
Interview: Redis blocking commands (KEYS) can be slow.
Watch cache invalidations — stale reads common.
terms: Data in RAM — bypass disk I/O. Redis, Memcached, SAP HANA.
RAM volatile — Redis RDB/AOF, cluster snapshot (S3).
Memory full — remove data via LRU policies.
Append-only file — logs every write, granular restore.
k5.visualCap: In-memory: RAM speed, volatile. RDB snapshot / AOF log + LRU eviction.

k6.name: Embedded databases — SQLite, DuckDB
k6.desc: Embedded databases run inside your app process with no separate server. SQLite: single file, full SQL, every phone has it. DuckDB: columnar, great for running SQL analytics on CSV/Parquet files locally.
k6.q: What are the limitations of SQLite? When does it reach its limits?
k6.qsub: How does DuckDB differ from SQLite? Why is it better for analytics?
k6.what:
Embedded databases run inside the app like a library — no server, no port, no setup. SQLite: file-based, ultra-portable (mobile, local apps, edge). DuckDB: analytical gold — columnar + direct SQL on Parquet — zero-copy ETL for data science.

Caveats: SQLite write concurrency limited (many nodes single-writer) — WAL mode improves reads. Embedded vs client-server: multi-process scale = server; local/edge analysis = embedded.
k6.analogy: Pocket diary vs bank branch: SQLite = pocket diary — in your pocket (app), no ID card (no login), the file is the diary. Bank branch (server DB) = formal counter, others have their own. DuckDB = pocket calculator for bookkeeping — analyzes all account books without a branch. Large team work = branch; local math = diary.
k6.why: Interview: "Where SQLite?" — local cache/local-first apps. DuckDB — buzz around modern analytics tooling. Embedded vs server trade-off — scale + concurrency versus simplicity.
gotchas: Just remember: embedded = app-library DB; SQLite file-perfect; DuckDB = columnar local analytics.
Interview: WAL mode = readers while writer.
S3 par DuckDB direct range scans — analytics cheap.
terms: Library inside the app — no server. SQLite, DuckDB.
SQLite concurrent reads + writer not blocked.
k6.visualCap: Embedded = app-internal library (SQLite file, DuckDB columnar). No server.

k7.name: Polyglot persistence — multiple DB types
k7.desc: Polyglot persistence means using different databases for different workloads. Postgres for core data, Redis for cache, Elasticsearch for search, S3 for files. Each database excels at what it does best.
k7.q: How do you decide which database to use for each part of your application?
k7.qsub: How do you keep multiple databases in sync? What role does CDC play?
k7.what:
Polyglot persistence = a single system, multiple data stores, each use-case gets the best tool: orders → Postgres, cart/session → Redis, search → Elasticsearch, analytics → ClickHouse. Fit-per-use – each workload has its own trade-off.

Cost: multiple systems = multiple ops + data sync (event-driven) + eventual consistency. Small team → start with a robust DB (Postgres+JSONB); adopt polyglot when patterns are clear. Only graph/vector/specialized needs justify a polyglot system.
k7.analogy: One person's house vs mansion kitchen: a small kitchen has a single stove (single DB) — simple. A large house: separate tandoor (search), separate fridge tray (cache), register (orders). Each zone has its own expert — but each new zone adds new staff + rule book. In a basic house run everything on one stove; add zones when you have many users.
k7.why: Interview: "why multiple databases?" — polyglot explanation + trap (premature polyglot). This is the honest system-design answer: store per concern, not per microservice.
gotchas: Remember this: polyglot = different needs, different stores; PG+JSONB as a base; watch operational cost.
Interview: a search use-case alone can justify polyglot.
Data movement between stores = events/CDC (eventual consistency).
terms: Different data needs = different stores — one app, many DBs.
Relational for orders, KV for carts, search engine for products.
Each microservice has its own DB — distributed transaction pain.
A robust DB (Postgres JSONB) — for minimal team size.
Postgres JSON column — document behavior in SQL.
k7.visualCap: Polyglot: Postgres orders + Redis cart + ES search + ware - fit per use. Cost conscious.

db-migrations.name: Database Migrations — schema versioning, zero-downtime, backward compatibility
db-migrations.desc: Database migrations version-control schema changes. Tools: Flyway (Java), Alembic (Python), Prisma Migrate (Node.js), golang-migrate. Zero-downtime: additive changes only (add column, not rename). Rollback strategy for each migration. Backward compatible: old code must work with new schema.
db-migrations.q: How do you perform a zero-downtime database migration? What is the expand-contract pattern?
db-migrations.qsub: What is the difference between forward-only migrations and reversible migrations? How do you handle column renames safely?
db-migrations.what:
Migrations make schema changes versioned, reproducible, reviewable — better than ad-hoc SQL. Each change is a numbered file: 001_create_users.sql. Tools (Flyway, Liquibase, ORM migrate) apply them in order and record them in the schema_migrations table.

Golden rules: additive first (new column/table) — backward compatible; remove old later. Expand & Contract: add column → deploy code → drop column. This is critical with rolling deployments. Down migrations provide a rollback option.
db-migrations.analogy: Small incremental commits vs big bang change: migrations are like kitchen renovation in small steps (add new wiring, then remove old). One file is one idea — reviewable, can be reverted. Without migrations — "ALTER on live DB at night" = cut table first, then code breaks. Expand & contract: add new wiring (additive) → everyone uses it → remove old.
db-migrations.why: Interview: "how to change schema safely?" — migrations + expand/contract. This is production ops 101 — reviewable DDL, rollback story. Follow-up: auto-apply in CI/CD pipeline.
gotchas: Remember this: migrations = versioned DDL; additive first, contract later; up/down pairs.
Interview: big ALTER on large tables = lock storm — use online tools (gh-ost/pt-osc).
Run migrations through code review + CI.
terms: Versioned schema change — SQL files in code repo.
db-migrations.visualCap: Versioned DDL files → runner → schema_migrations table. Expand, then contract.

multi-tenancy.name: Multi-tenancy patterns — shared DB, schema-per-tenant, DB-per-tenant
multi-tenancy.desc: Shared DB: all tenants in same tables with tenant_id column (cheapest, hardest to isolate). Schema-per-tenant: separate schemas in one DB (good isolation, moderate cost). DB-per-tenant: fully isolated (highest cost, easiest to customize). Row-Level Security (RLS) enforces tenant isolation at DB level.
multi-tenancy.q: What are the tradeoffs between shared DB, schema-per-tenant, and DB-per-tenant?
multi-tenancy.qsub: How does Row-Level Security enforce tenant isolation? When would you choose DB-per-tenant over shared DB?
multi-tenancy.what:
Multi-tenancy = a SaaS system, many customers, data isolated. Levels: (1) pooled — a single DB with a tenant_id column; cheap + simple, but forgetting WHERE leads to data leak (RLS prevents that). (2) schema-per-tenant — clean boundary, more migrations. (3) DB-per-tenant — maximum isolation + cost, enterprise grade.

Pick: small-medium users → pooled + RLS; large/regulatory accounts → schema or DB per tenant. Tenant data leak is a nightmare — isolation design must be addressed early.
multi-tenancy.analogy: Apartment building rooms: pooled = a huge common office, each zone has its own desk + lock (tenant_id + RLS door guard — without asking, a person can only access its zone). Schema-per-tenant = each family gets its own floor (clean, their belongings). DB-per-tenant = separate bungalow — full ownership, expensive. The guard (RLS) prevents leaks in the pooled model.
multi-tenancy.why: SaaS interview: "how do you isolate tenants?" — three models + trade-off + PostgreSQL RLS. This is an important architectural point for security and ops scaling. "Forgetting WHERE tenant_id" — RLS provides an automatic guard.
gotchas: Remember this: pooled+tenant_id (RLS), schema-per, db-per — isolation vs cost ladder.
Interview: pooled needs RLS — forgetting WHERE leads to leak.
Tenant migration later is hard — design early.
terms: A software with many customers (tenants) — data separated.
Pooled (shared DB, tenant_id), Schema-per-tenant, Separate DB.
The address for the pooled model — used in every query.
Separate schema per customer — clean boundary, moderate ops.
PostgreSQL Row-Level Security — automatically filters by tenant_id (no WHERE needed).
multi-tenancy.visualCap: Pooled (tenant_id + RLS) vs Schema-per-tenant vs DB-per-tenant.
codeSwap: Sab queries automatically filtered — WHERE bhoolne par bhi.
All queries are filtered automatically — even if you forget WHERE.

perf7.name: Monitoring — pg_stat_statements, cache hit ratio
perf7.desc: Monitoring tracks key health signals. Most important metrics: query latency p95/p99, active connections, cache hit rate (>95% target), disk I/O, replication lag. PostgreSQL built-in views expose all of this.
perf7.q: What are the most important database metrics to monitor in production?
perf7.qsub: How do you use pg_stat_statements to find the slowest queries?
perf7.what:
DB monitoring = keep the system’s river visible. Metrics: CPU, connections (need pooling), cache hit ratio (>95%), slow queries (in logs), replication lag (seconds), disk I/O/space. Tools: pg_stat_activity, Prometheus + Grafana, CloudWatch.

Detect issues before they trigger alerts (page bloat, connection starvation) so users don’t notice. SLO: p95 latency, error rate. Monitoring provides indexing/planning targets — not guesses.
perf7.analogy: Home safety meter board: monitoring = each gauge (electricity, water, pressure) on a dashboard. Slow-query log = "which water tap is opened the most" (which query is greedy). Alert = SMS when water pressure drops. PgBouncer = a door that lets 10 people in — instead of 100 separate doors (connections) in a house.
perf7.why: Core production ops — "DB is slow, what’s the first thing you do?" → look at metrics + slow query log. Practical interview answer: derive index from monitoring insight, pool connections, set alert thresholds.
gotchas: Remember this: monitor = CPU/conn/hit/lag/slow; detect before alerts; PgBouncer for connections.
Interview: connection leakage is common — use a pool.
Watch autovacuum lag — bloat makes tables slow.
terms: DB health visibility — metrics, logs, dashboards.
CPU, connections, cache hit, slow queries, replication lag, disk.
Queries exceeding certain ms — tuning targets.
Notifications based on rules — pings, thresholds.
perf7.visualCap: Monitor: CPU, connections, hit ratio, slow logs, lag → dashboards + alerts.

perf3.name: Connection pooling — PgBouncer, HikariCP
perf3.desc: Opening a new DB connection takes 5-100ms and PostgreSQL spawns a process. Connection pooling keeps a fixed number of connections open and reuses them. Optimal pool size is ~2x CPU cores.
perf3.q: Why is connection pooling necessary? What happens without it?
perf3.qsub: What is the optimal connection pool size? Why does more connections sometimes mean worse performance?
perf3.what:
Creating a new DB connection for each query costs TCP + auth + worker + memory. A connection pool is a bucket of ready-made connections — the app borrows, uses, and returns them. Sustained throughput without connection churn.

Pool size: more connections = more workers — but not beyond the CPU. Approximate formula: (core*2) + effective disk. 10k connections = memory burn + thundering herd. PgBouncer = external pooler (transaction vs session pooling).
perf3.analogy: Swimming pool lanes: each swimmer digging a new pool (new connection) — madness. The pool provides 20 ready lanes; a person takes one, swims, and returns it. More lanes cost money and crowd space; fewer is not possible. A booking agency (PgBouncer) keeps lanes ready for the app — instantly for each transaction.
perf3.why: Interview: "app slow — DB connection exhaustion" answer is a pool. Pool size + PgBouncer — production baseline. This is part of app-scale basics.
gotchas: Just remember: pool = reusable connections; size=(core*2)+disk; PgBouncer = external pooler.
Interview: session pooling vs transaction pooling difference.
Connection leakage (not returned) = slow exhaustion.
terms: DB connections reusable set — a new one is not created for each request.
TCP handshake + auth + memory — new connection expensive.
Around the CPU — (core*2)+disk; thousands of connections cause thrashing.
PG connection pooler — transaction pooling mode.
Java default — sane defaults + fast borrow.
perf3.visualCap: App reuses pooled connections — no TCP/auth per request. Pool size bound.

perf5.name: Backup & recovery — PITR via WAL, RPO/RTO
perf5.desc: PITR (Point-in-Time Recovery) restores to any specific moment using a base backup + archived WAL files. RPO = max data loss. RTO = recovery time. Test your backups by actually restoring them.
perf5.q: How does Point-in-Time Recovery work in PostgreSQL?
perf5.qsub: What is the difference between RPO and RTO? How do they influence backup strategy?
perf5.what:
Backup = a copy for disaster recovery. PITR (PostgreSQL): base backup + WAL archiving — restore at any moment (recovers data accidentally deleted). Full base + incremental WAL — balanced.

Define RPO (maximum data loss) vs RTO (time to be back online). Tested restores = real backup (always drill) — otherwise it's a backup of a backup. Cloud: RDS snapshots + built-in PITR.
perf5.analogy: Life’s diamond locker + CCTV: backup = a photo of the diamond in the locker (full copy). PITR = CCTV feed that records every second (WAL) — restore any second’s moment (shows exactly when a theft occurred). If the locker photo becomes outdated, use the CCTV moment. Drill = each month "open a new locker and match the photo" — without a drill the backup is just paper.
perf5.why: Interview backup question: "how do you protect against data loss?" — PITR + tested restore. RPO/RTO vocabulary signals senior-level competence. This is non-negotiable for ops.
gotchas: Just remember: backup = base + WAL; PITR = any second; RPO/RTO define + drill.
Interview: untested backup = no backup.
WAL archive retention — recovery window decides.
terms: Copy of data stored elsewhere — for restore.
Point-in-Time Recovery — restore to any moment.
Each WAL segment stored on S3 — continuous log.
How much data loss is tolerable / how quickly to be back up.
perf5.visualCap: Base backup + WAL archive → restore at any point. RPO/RTO define + drill.

perf8.name: Migration strategies — Expand-Migrate-Contract
perf8.desc: Schema migrations in production are dangerous. Safe strategy: Expand (add new column), Migrate (backfill in batches), Contract (drop old column). Tools like gh-ost and pgroll do online migrations with no locking.
perf8.q: What is the Expand-Migrate-Contract pattern? Why is it safer than direct ALTER TABLE?
perf8.qsub: How does gh-ost perform online schema changes on MySQL without locking?
perf8.what:
Zero-downtime schema change = Expand & Contract: 1) expand — additive column/table (backfill slowly), 2) deploy code that uses the new schema, 3) contract — remove the old one. Direct ALTER on a large table = lock storm (writes stop).

Online tools (gh-ost, pt-osc) create a ghost table, copy data, sync binlog, and swap — without a long lock. The default answer for tables with over 1 M rows.
perf8.analogy: Flyover bridge repair: closing the road directly = jam (lock). Expand & contract = first build a new lane (additive), move traffic to the new lane, then close the old lane (drop). gh-ost = construction where small nudges happen in a trench; live traffic does not stop. Backfill = filling old data into the new format — in batches, not blocking.
perf8.why: Interview: "add a column to a huge table without downtime?" — expand/contract + online DDL tools. This is the senior answer for production migrations — avoids lock storms.
gotchas: Just remember: expand → deploy → contract; gh-ost/pt-osc = copy+swap; large ALTER = lock storm.
Interview: NOT NULL default on huge table — PG 11+ default safe-ish, lock still.
Backfill always in batches + monitor.
terms: Additive first, deploy, remove old later — zero downtime.
Writes also go to the new column — old readers still work.
gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change — copy + swap, without lock.
Direct ALTER on big table = table lock = downtime.
Populate the new column with old data — batched jobs.
perf8.visualCap: Expand (add) → deploy → contract (drop). No long lock; ghost swap online.

l5.name: Security — SQL injection, RBAC, RLS
l5.desc: SQL injection is the #1 database attack. ALWAYS use parameterized queries. RBAC gives minimum required privileges. Row-Level Security in PostgreSQL enforces which rows each user can see at the database level.
l5.q: How do you prevent SQL injection? Why are parameterized queries essential?
l5.qsub: How does Row-Level Security work in PostgreSQL for multi-tenant applications?
l5.what:
SQL injection = hidden attacker code inside SQL: WHERE email = 'admin' OR '1'='1' — never build a query with string concatenation. Prepared statements are key: the SQL skeleton is parsed first, then values are bound — injection becomes impossible (values never become SQL).

Access: RBAC — user/role permission mapping; RLS — row-level gating in SQL (multi-tenant). Least privilege — do not give the app user DROP rights. Sanitization is a second line; parameter binding is the main defense.
l5.analogy: Ticket counter asking for "name": concatenation = the clerk writes the name directly into the register — if the name is "Rahul; give all money" the register processes it (injection!). Prepared — the form is fixed first, the name goes only into a value box — "Rahul;..." is just a value, not a command. RLS = each window has its own door; the key (policy) can be opened only by its own group.
l5.why: Security interview first question — remember SQLi? Prepared statements + ORM provide a safe path. RLS/RBAC add access-level sophistication. This gives a complete answer to "how would you secure the DB" in one line.
gotchas: Just remember: prepared statements = injection-free; RBAC roles; RLS rows; least privilege.
Interview: stored procedures also require parameters — no concatenation.
ORM raw queries use the same prepared path.
terms: Injecting hidden attacker code into the app’s SQL.
Query skeleton plus separate parameters — SQL parsing is fixed.
Values are bound, never concatenated as strings.
Row Level Security — row visibility per policy.
Only as much access as needed for the job.
l5.visualCap: String concat = injection door open. Prepared = params only, SQL fixed. RLS gates rows.
codeSwap: value hi value rahi, SQL nahi bani.
only the value remained, no SQL was built.

l6.name: N+1 problem — detection, eager loading, DataLoader
l6.desc: The N+1 problem: load a list (1 query) then load details for each item (N queries). 100 posts + comments = 101 queries. Fix: eager loading with JOINs or batch loading with DataLoader.
l6.q: What is the N+1 query problem? How do you detect and fix it?
l6.qsub: How does DataLoader in JavaScript batch database queries within a single event loop tick?
l6.what:
N+1: one query for the root record, then one query for each of the 100 child records — slow. Example: SELECT posts + for each post SELECT comments.

Fixes: JOIN (rows flat — remember pagination), batch WHERE id IN (...), ORM eager loading (with/eager), DataLoader-style queue batching. Only read path — write path is rare.
l6.analogy: Grocery delivery: N+1 = one rickshaw per house (N rickshaws) — wasteful. Batch = a single rickshaw for the whole village list (WHERE city IN) — one trip. JOIN = a single invoice that contains both goods and receipts. DataLoader = collect all orders first then deliver in one go. Fewer network hops = app fast.
l6.why: Interview "Why is the app's API slow?" — N+1 classic. ORM eager loading + batch IN — correct answer. This is also the most common performance bug in performance debugging.
gotchas: Just remember: N+1 = N child queries; JOIN/IN/eager = fix; DataLoader = batching.
Interview: JOIN pagination can produce duplicate rows on offset.
Lazy loading can hide N+1 — profile queries.
terms: 1 query for root + N queries for children — many network hops.
Fetch children up front — ORM joins/with.
Parent and children in a single query (ORM).
IN (ids…) — children in a single query.
GraphQL/Node — batching and cache per request.
l6.visualCap: N+1: 1 + N queries. Fix: JOIN / IN batch / eager load — 1-2 queries.

sd1.name: URL Shortener DB — sharding, caching, pre-generated keys
sd1.q: How would you design the database layer for a URL shortener at scale?
sd1.qsub: Why would you pre-generate short codes in batches instead of generating on each write?
sd1.what:
URL shortener design (tinyurl): POST long URL → return abc123; GET /abc123 → 301 Location redirect. Storage: short_code PK + long_url + created_at + clicks.

Code: auto-increment id → base62 encode (short, no ugly chars). DB: mapping table (hash key = code). Caching: hot URLs Redis (read-heavy: 99% reads). Expiry/cleanup + analytics counters. Collision: same long URL → upsert same code. Hash (MD5) + prefix = common — collisions are handled.
sd1.analogy: Library's small slip: instead of a long name use a "shelf-code" — short. "Take slip A12B3" then look up in table, get the long name (redirect). Cache provides 301 so no repeated lookup. Writer (0.1% writes) does little work — readers (99.9%) dominate.
sd1.why: Classic system design question — scale calculations (reads/writes), storage, cache, redirect semantics. Hash vs base62, collision, TTL — appears in every interview.
gotchas: Just remember: encode id → base62; code as PK; Redis cache; 301 = permanent.
Interview: 301 is cacheable — short URL should not change.
Bloom filter collision check — uses very little memory.
terms: Different URLs same short code — ensure unique row first.
Set of all used codes — fast collision check.
sd1.visualCap: Encode id → base62. Mapping store + Redis cache → 301 redirect.

sd3.name: Chat/Messaging DB — conversation partitioning, ordering
sd3.q: How do you ensure message ordering in a distributed chat system?
sd3.qsub: Why shard by conversation ID instead of user ID? What are the trade-offs?
sd3.what:
Chat system design: send message → store (Postgres/Cassandra) + push via WebSocket. conversation_id fixed slot; messages ORDER BY ts. Fan-out: group chat = message to N members — queue at scale.

Storage choices: 1:1 chat = single row per message; group big threads = shared + cursor (no per-member copy). Unread counts = Redis counters. Presence = heartbeat → Redis TTL, online list. Read receipts = last_read_ts per user.
sd3.analogy: Hostel mess notice board + messenger: write (store), immediate announcement (WebSocket) to everyone in the group. Message is written once, everyone reads from their inbox — no per-person copy (shared document + cursor). Unread = "how far each member has read" (Redis counter). Online = "activity in the last 2 minutes" via heartbeat.
sd3.why: System design favorite — like WhatsApp/Discord. Real-time, fan-out, presence, unread — best practice for multi-component design. Involves microservices, queues, and cache.
gotchas: Just remember: store + WS push; fan-out queue; presence via Redis heartbeat; unread per-read cursor.
Interview: message ordering = ts + per-conversation seq.
At-least-once + idempotency for reconnect resends.
terms: WebSocket push — large scale with load balancer + fan-out.
One message to many receivers — queues/read replicas.
sd3.visualCap: Send → store + WS push. Fan-out via queue. Presence via Redis heartbeats.

sd2.name: News Feed DB — push vs pull, celebrity handling
sd2.q: What is the difference between fan-out-on-write and fan-out-on-read?
sd2.qsub: How do Twitter and Instagram handle celebrity accounts with millions of followers?
sd2.what:
News feed design = each user’s personal timeline. Fan-out on write: as soon as a post arrives, insert it into followers’ Redis lists — reads fast; but for a celebrity? 100M followers = 100M writes. Fan-out on read: on read, merge influencer feeds — hot users fast, celebrities cheap. Hybrid best: normal users use write-fanout, celebrities use read-merge.

Feed cache: per-user Redis list (post IDs) + hydrate details (cache + DB). Ranking: recency × engagement. Pagination: cursor by ID.
sd2.analogy: Tea stall group news chain: fan-out-on-write = send to each friend’s house in advance (immediate news for everyone) — but superstar news everywhere is exhausting. Read-merge = only fetch for big names when reading. Hybrid = pre-built list for regular friends, read-time check for celebrities. Timeline = calendar; cursor = unread markers.
sd2.why: Twitter/IG design interview classic question — fan-out strategies + Redis feed + ranking. Distributed caching + event-driven complete network. "Why not just DB query?" — merging friends per request is hard.
gotchas: Just remember: fan-out on write = pre-built feeds; celebrities read-merge; Redis list per user.
Interview: delete/update post = feed cleanup (fan-out pain).
Cursor pagination for feeds, not offset.
terms: Each user’s personalized timeline — posts from followed users.
Insert into followers’ feeds as soon as the post is created — reads cheap.
Merge at serve time — hot users okay, celebrities also fine.
Redis list per user — precomputed timeline.
sd2.visualCap: Write-fanout → per-user Redis feed. Celebrity = read-time merge (hybrid).
